items.title: The Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) - A Revised Theory for Trust Calibration in Automation and Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Calibrated trust is considered an important factor for human-system interaction in decision-making. However, definitions of calibrated trust are heterogeneous and research often lacks conceptual clarity. In our work, we conducted a theoretical integration to summarize approaches defining and operationalizing calibrated trust in automation and AI. We then mapped these approaches onto the trust development process that builds on the Trustworthiness Assessment Model (Schlicker, Baum, et al., 2025) and the Organizational Trust Model (Mayer et al., 1995). The resulting Trust Calibration Points Framework (TCa-P) offers theoretical clarity and actionable insights for improving trust calibration by identifying six calibration points that can be calibrated to optimize joint human-system performance, and, as a consequence, effective human oversight: maximum joint performance benchmarking, trustworthiness assessment, alignment of individual standards, risk-benefit assessment, dispositions, and behavioral adaptation. The TCa-P emphasizes that trust calibration is not monolithic but instead happens at different points along the trust development process.

items.title: The Value Semantics Layer: Enabling Machine-Understandable Databases for Agentic AI
items.abstract: As data systems increasingly support autonomous LLM-powered agents alongside human analysts, they require richer semantic infrastructure bridging analytical concepts and analytical operations. Existing metadata systems expose schemas, catalogs, lineage, and governance information, but provide limited support for representing operational semantics. We propose the Value Semantics Layer (VSL), an architectural abstraction that externalizes value semantics as persistent, planner-visible infrastructure. VSL introduces Value Semantic Types (VSTs), reusable operational semantic assertions capturing distributional, relational, process, quantitative, and policy-grounded semantics. Unlike descriptive metadata, VSTs enable planners to validate analytical operations, select appropriate operators, and guide analytical workflows. We present the motivation, formalization, architecture, and prototype realizations of VSL, and outline a research agenda toward AI-native semantic infrastructure for analytical systems.

items.title: The Xaant Resting Autonomic Signature (X-RAS): prospective clinical validation of an autonomic biomarker for anxiety and depressive disorders
items.abstract: Background Anxiety and depressive disorders affect over 500 million people globally, with a treatment gap exceeding 75% in low- and middle-income countries. Current diagnostic frameworks rely on clinical interview and self-report, with test–retest reliability of 0.20 to 0.67 for these disorders in DSM-5 field trials. Autonomic nervous system dysregulation is a well-established biological correlate of anxiety and depression. We report the first, to our knowledge, prospective clinical validation of an autonomic biomarker-based artificial intelligence system against a blinded psychiatrist reference standard in routine clinical practice. Methods We conducted a prospective, two-site diagnostic accuracy study at tertiary hospitals in Delhi and Kerala, India (CTRI/2023/07/054984). The Xaant Resting Autonomic Signature (X-RAS) platform, a three-layer LSTM with self-attention previously developed on an independent cohort of 2,349 participants and frozen prior to the trial, analysed electrodermal activity and blood volume pulse from 15-minute resting-state recordings and produced a four-class diagnostic classification. Of 180 participants enrolled, 170 completed the protocol. Out of these, 114 clinical participants with DSM-5 depression, anxiety, or comorbid disorders, and 56 reference group participants recruited from a long-term meditation practice tradition were considered. The reference standard was the DSM-5 diagnosis established by the site psychiatrist, who was blinded to the platform output. The primary outcome was Cohen's kappa for AI-psychiatrist diagnostic agreement within the clinical cohort. Results Within the clinical cohort, the platform achieved 93.0% agreement with clinical diagnosis (κ = 0.884, 95% CI 0.789 to 0.956), with 100% sensitivity for generalised anxiety disorder (GAD) detection in the GAD subgroup (n = 15, 95% CI 78.2 to 100). All eight classification disagreements fell along the depression–comorbid boundary, and the AI classification agreed with the patient's own self-categorisation in five of the eight. Performance was consistent across the two sites (Delhi 94.6%, Kerala 91.4%, p = 0.527) and across age, sex, and education subgroups. Classical autonomic markers separated the clinical and reference groups with moderate to large effect sizes (d = 0.53 to 0.84). Two of the physiological constructs of the development-cohort, namely Hypoactivity and Experience, were reproduced at the group level in independently diagnosed patients. A per-minute slope analysis of the tonic EDA signal showed a transdiagnostic reversal, where the baseline settled downward during rest in the reference group and drifted upward across all three clinical subgroups (Kruskal–Wallis p = 3.0 × 10⁻²²). Conclusions Resting-state autonomic AI analysis provides objective diagnostic support for anxiety and depressive disorders, with Cohen’s κ = 0.884 (95% CI 0.789 to 0.956) against psychiatrist-assigned DSM-5 diagnoses in routine outpatient practice. Direct comparison with published inter-rater or test-retest reliability estimates is not appropriate given differences in methodology and reference standards. The platform's low cost, portability, and suitability for non-specialist operators support scalability in resource-limited settings. External validation in primary care, community, telehealth, and non-Indian populations is the next step for the programme. Trial registration: Clinical Trials Registry of India, CTRI/2023/07/054984, registered July 2023.

items.title: Think Before You Code: A Benchmark for Testing LLMs on Software Engineering Deliberation
items.abstract: Think Before You Code (TBYC) is a benchmark pipeline for studying whether code-focused language models can reason about software issues in ways that resemble human engineering deliberation. The benchmark curates GitHub issue discussions into structured records, extracts human discussion artifacts such as problems, solutions, constraints, rationales, and trade-offs, and then prompts models to generate issue-level "thoughts" using retrieved code context and few-shot examples. It converts model responses back into the same artifact space and evaluates them against human annotations using complementary metrics for artifact type detection, metadata matching, tag overlap, and semantic summary similarity. Beyond scoring, this study includes visualization, leaderboard, and baseline tools that make it possible to compare models, prompting strategies, and extraction methods across repositories and issues. Think Before You Code is an end-to-end evaluation environment for measuring how closely LLM software reasoning aligns with human strategic judgment.

items.title: Three Modernisations, Five Commons and Three Progressive Stages: A Case Study of School–Enterprise Collaborative Training of Field Engineers in a Chinese Higher Vocational College
items.abstract: Graduates of vocational programmes in the new-generation information technology industry often match employers’ job requirements poorly, and the transition from classroom practice to real work remains difficult. In response to China’s national special training plan for field engineers, Xi’an Vocational and Technical College and Beijing New World Times Science and Technology Co., Ltd. established a joint field-engineer programme for Java development and technical support posts. This article presents a qualitative case study of that programme, based on documentary analysis of project records and institutional reports interpreted through research on workplace learning and boundary crossing. The programme rests on three supports (a substantive governance organisation, a digital industry-data platform and institutionalised standards), a five-part closed loop in which school and enterprise jointly select entrants, teach, build learning resources, manage the process and evaluate results, and a three-stage practical sequence that moves students from post recognition on campus, through project rotation in the enterprise, to certified post-holding. Reported outputs include donated training equipment, jointly developed digital teaching resources, competition awards and high first-destination employment, although these figures come from the programme’s own records and have not been independently verified. The analysis suggests that institutionalised rights and responsibilities, deliberate support for crossing the boundary between school and work, and continuous feedback from industry data are the features most likely to transfer to other colleges. Limitations and directions for outcome-focused research are discussed.

items.title: TikTok Goes the Doomsday Clock—Digital Practices of Dealing with Nuclear Danger
items.abstract: In June 2025 and February 2026, the wars involving the United States, Israel and Iran led to content about nuclear war being posted on social media, particularly on TikTok and Instagram. In this article, I ask what practices social media creators are enacting to deal with perceived nuclear danger and explore how the practices relate to the struggle for agency to participate in international politics. I utilised practice theory and digital ethnography to analyse 146 short videos, allowing me particularly to expand the relations of practice theory with visualities, the study of popular culture and world politics, sociotechnical imaginaries, and workshops as methodology. I find that practices that digital creators enact can be described as nuclear nihilism, postapocalyptic imagining, nuclear education, and social media self-reflection. While nuclear nihilism describes the tendency to approach nuclear danger with indifference rather than anxiety, postapocalyptic imaginaries are visual depictions of an often romanticised post–nuclear war landscape. Nuclear education aims to spread knowledge about nuclear weapons, and self-reflection about social media addresses the absurdity of producing videos on nuclear war at all. The role of agency is ambivalent: Whereas some creators expect to possess hegemonic agency in a postapocalyptic reality, others grieve about their missing agency regarding nuclear weapons politics and about changing life during a permacrisis at large.

items.title: Time to learn? A qualitative interview study on organizational learning time from employee's perspectives
items.abstract: Introduction This qualitative study aimed to examine organizational learning time as a potential measure to facilitate deliberative informal learning within a formally organized frame and to address lack of time as a main barrier to learning. Organizational learning time refers to a fixed amount of time that employers allocate to employees, allowing them to self-directedly, intentionally, and informally engage with work-related topics on a voluntary basis. Methods Because organizational learning time has not yet been systematically studied, we conducted 10 semi-structured interviews with German-speaking employees from various industries. The goal was to explore their attitudes toward a hypothetical introduction of 1 hour of learning time per week within their organization and to identify potential factors influencing its use. We analyzed the data using content-structuring qualitative content analysis, combining deductive categories with inductively developed subcategories. Results Overall, participants had positive attitudes toward organizational learning time and expected both personal development and organizational benefits. Concerns about time in competition with day-to-day business and social acceptance among colleagues emerged as the most frequently mentioned factors influencing anticipated use. Parallels with antecedents of informal learning were identified. Discussion Despite limited generalizability and the intention-behavior gap, the study provides initial insights into anticipated conditions under which organizational learning time might be used successfully. Future research could examine whether it may be particularly useful in organizations where learning is not yet regarded as an integral part of work. While (reactive) informal learning inevitably occurs during work processes, organizational learning time might help organizations to create space for (deliberative) informal learning outside of day-to-day operations. This allows employees to prepare for the rapidly changing demands of the workplace.

items.title: Title and Abstract Screening for Systematic Reviews with Jev, a Decision Model: Comparison with Generative Large Language Models
items.abstract: We evaluated Jev, a non-generative decision model, for title and abstract screening using 4527 records from two systematic reviews of bipolar disorder treatments previously used in our 2024 Journal of Medical Internet Research study. Human decisions to retain records for full-text assessment served as the reference. In the primary analysis, Jev answered yes-or-no questions (Noul); at a prespecified 50% cutoff, sensitivity and specificity were 99.6% and 98.9% for light therapy and 93.2% and 93.5% for adjunctive pharmacotherapy. For direct model comparison, Jev used explicit include/exclude options (Choice) and the same prompts as GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra. Jev Choice achieved sensitivity and specificity similar to or higher than those of GPT-5 mini and GPT-6 Astra, while API charges per 1000 records were US$0.043 for Jev, US$0.57 for GPT-5 mini, and US$7.39 for GPT-6 Astra. Jev retained all reports ultimately included in both reviews across all tested conditions and runs. Although these findings do not establish that decision models can replace human reviewers, they support Jev as a promising, low-cost alternative to the tested generative LLM configurations for assisting human title and abstract screening. Independent validation across diverse review topics is needed to assess Jev’s generalizability and utility in human-supervised screening workflows.

items.title: Tokenaholics: The New Silent Addiction of the Artificial Intelligence Era
items.abstract: The expansion of generative artificial intelligence makes it necessary to distinguish computational consumption, adoption, and problematic dependence. This article proposes Tokenaholics as an exploratory concept without diagnostic equivalence and combines an interdisciplinary critical review with secondary analysis of public aggregates from 2025 and 2026. It examines Anthropic usage profiles by country and occupational group, Vercel daily token and spending shares, and GitHub indicators. K-means using five variables selects a two-group partition among 121 countries, with limited separation (silhouette of 0.308). The GitHub– Anthropic comparison matches eight of the ten countries in the GitHub table. Computer and mathematical occupations have published shares of 23.80% in chat and 28.17% in the API in May 2026; these measures retain each channel’s denominator. Temporal evaluation of Ridge and three baselines does not support stable predictive superiority. Budget scenarios for 2027 combine token quantity and effective price under a constant mix. The findings describe geographic heterogeneity, differences between channels, and distinct distributions of tokens and expenditure. These results characterize the sociotechnical context without operationalizing or validating Tokenaholics, estimating the prevalence of dependence, or identifying causality. The contribution to computer science is to connect a bounded conceptual definition with reproducible analytical procedures and a future agenda for evaluating regulation, verification, and functional impairment.

items.title: Tools at the tempo of teaching: Vibe engineering an LMS-embedded Fishbowl tool
items.abstract: Background The Fishbowl is a discussion format: an inner ring discusses a prompt while an outer ring observes and swaps in (Bermudez, n.d.). When it runs well, the interaction reaches the interactive tier of Chi and Wylie’s (2014) ICAP framework, most strongly linked to deep learning. Novice teachers struggle to orchestrate so complex a discussion and often avoid it or run it as procedural theatre (Dillenbourg, 2002), while students lack the scaffolding to grasp what good discussion looks like or to notice their participation in real time. Fixed-seat rooms make the concentric-ring layout harder to set up. The shift An LMS-embedded learning tool can address these problems by scaffolding through the interface itself: built-in phase sequencing and role-specific views support teachers as drivers rather than executors (Dillenbourg, 2013), while giving students concrete moves for good discussion and cues to notice their participation. Such a tool was never technically impossible, only unjustifiable, requiring a software team and budget cycle for one learning activity. Generative AI now lets a single learning designer (LD) author and revise a version between deliveries, so refinement moves at the tempo of teaching rather than procurement. However, unmediated “vibe coding” is fragile across accessibility, security, and pedagogical validity. Vibe engineering (Willison, 2025) is the discipline that makes the speed safe. Development snapshot Vibe engineering can be brought to education by drawing on Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (CSCL) orchestration and collaboration-script theory (Fischer et al., 2013; Kollar et al., 2006): balancing under- and over-scripting (Dillenbourg, 2002), preserving intrinsic script constraints (Dillenbourg & Tchounikine, 2007), and scaffolding transactive discourse (Fischer et al., 2013). Each version is audited in a separate AI session against accessibility and security checklists, while pedagogical validity is judged by the LD through CSCL orchestration principles and classroom observation. Every update ships as one small static HTML file, stored centrally with no student data and no runtime AI, so it propagates automatically to every unit that uses it. Poster experience Live demonstration on two adjacent devices: the projected Fishbowl discussion phase (teacher-facing) alongside the private ideas phase (student-facing). Annotated walkthrough of core design elements with their theoretical warrants. A few major versions showing how the tool evolved, with a QR link to selected prompt history. The accessibility and security checklists, with a QR link to the open-source versions. Relevance to the theme: Human-centred learning design The Fishbowl builds connection through structured dialogue, and the tool preserves that priority. It orchestrates the room without mediating the conversation, and the interface directs student attention to peers rather than screens. The approach is not specific to one activity: in principle, any collaboration script an LD can specify pedagogically could be authored at teaching tempo (cf. Holstein et al., 2019). Next steps The tool will run across teaching periods in 2026, with observations of orchestration load, participation, and facilitator experience feeding back into design rationales, checklists, and successive versions. The two checklists will be released as open-source, citable Markdown artefacts for the LD community.

items.title: Toward an epistemic ceiling: Collaboration structure, engagement depth, and knowledge activation in an exploratory study of interdisciplinary educator preparation for AI
items.abstract: This exploratory study examines how collaboration structures and engagement processes are associated with interdisciplinary knowledge construction among pre-service professionals engaged in AI-focused instructional design. There is not enough empirical evidence about professional collaboration when designing AI-integrated supports for diverse learners (Martinez-Maldonado et al., 2021; Wan et al., 2021). Little is known about how participation structures relate to the depth of cognitive engagement and knowledge integration that emerges during that process. This study used an exploratory, process-oriented discourse analysis that combined qualitative turn-level coding with descriptive frequencies. The researchers analyzed video-recorded collaborative discourse among pre-service special education teachers and pre-service school psychologists (N = 14) from an interdisciplinary graduate seminar focused on AI-integrated instructional design. The analysis used turn-level coding of participation patterns, cognitive and metacognitive engagement, and activation of an expanded Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge (TPACK) framework. The expanded framework incorporates Psychological Knowledge (PsychK) and Interdisciplinary Knowledge (IK). The study examined 3111 analytic turns across three interdisciplinary groups. It explored how participation distribution and cross-disciplinary exchange related to epistemic depth during collaboration. Groups with more distributed participation and more cross-disciplinary interaction tended to engage more often in high-level cognitive and metacognitive processes. They also showed broader combined activation of PsychK and IK related to AI tool use, learner variability, and ethical considerations. Groups with more concentrated participation tended toward procedural or discipline-specific reasoning, with limited activation of PsychK and IK. These patterns suggest that collaboration structure may play a role in shaping the kinds of professional knowledge that become salient during AI-focused interdisciplinary work. The study involved three groups in one seminar, its patterns describe these groups and should not be generalized. Group composition by discipline is a plausible alternative explanation for some of them. This exploratory study conceptualized interdisciplinary collaboration as an epistemic practice. It offered empirical insight into how professional knowledge may be negotiated under conditions of AI-mediated educational change. It proposed the epistemic ceiling as an exploratory theoretical proposition for future testing. The findings have implications for interdisciplinary educator preparation programs that aim to support ethical and inclusive AI integration as a collective, relational process. Future research with larger and more diverse samples could examine whether these patterns generalize across institutional and professional contexts.

items.title: Towards human-centred agentic AI mentoring ecosystems for female cybersecurity students
items.abstract: Women remain underrepresented in cybersecurity higher education and the workforce, with participation and retention influenced by confidence, belonging, professional identity, mentoring, and career readiness. While Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly supporting technical learning in cybersecurity, its potential to enhance students’ broader development remains underexplored. This conceptual position paper proposes a Human + Agentic AI mentoring ecosystem in which Agentic AI mentors complement, rather than replace, human mentors, educators, peers, and professional communities. Integrating Social Cognitive Career Theory (SCCT), women in cybersecurity literature, and human-centred AI design, we present a conceptual framework and design implications for Agentic AI mentoring that supports confidence, belonging, professional identity, career readiness and workforce transition. The framework extends AI beyond technical tutoring towards human-centred, co-designed mentoring across academic, social, and professional dimensions.

items.title: Transfer Once, Ask Locally: Compact Audio-Visual Memory for On-Device Question Answering
items.abstract: Audio-visual question answering on lightweight user devices requires balancing speed, memory usage, privacy, and communication. One approach is to run audio-visual encoders on a server and a lightweight language decoder on the user device, keeping questions local while offloading media encoding. However, transferring and processing the full multimodal representation remains costly. We propose a training-free, query-agnostic token pruning framework that constructs a compact, reusable memory before transmission. We define video spatio-temporal blocks and aligned audio windows as players and estimate their importance through Monte Carlo Shapley valuation. We use an embedding coverage objective that combines query-independent utility with cross-modal redundancy calibration and rewards unimodal diversity through marginal coverage gains. We retain the original token embeddings of high-scoring players under a limited token budget and transfer the resulting memory once for reuse across subsequent local questions. Experiments on Video-MME, Daily-Omni, and Video-Holmes using video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) and video-SALMONN 2 Pro (4B) show that our method achieves the best or tied-best QA accuracy among the compared compression methods across all evaluated settings. On Daily-Omni with video-SALMONN 2+ (3B) at 80\% pruning, our method improves accuracy by 12.86--14.62 percentage points over these methods while achieving the lowest device-side LLM prefill and decoding latency, with up to $1.92\times$ decoding speedup at comparable embedding memory usage.

items.title: TRANSFORMATION OF THE MOTIVATIONAL SPHERE OF HIGHER EDUCATION STUDENTS WITHIN THE SYSTEM OF SUBJECT-SUBJECT INTERACTION
items.abstract: The scientific article investigates the complex problem of the formation and dynamics of motivation in the educational and professional activity of university students within the framework of ongoing educational reforms. The study aims to determine the specific psychological and pedagogical features of students’ learning motives development and to substantiate a system of effective tools, conditions, and factors for increasing their cognitive and professional activity during their university studies. A complex of scientific methods was applied, including a systematic theoretical analysis of psychological literature and an empirical research project (surveying and diagnosing) involving approximately 300 1st, 2nd, and 4th-year students of Vinnytsia Mykhailo Kotsiubynskyi State Pedagogical University, alongside university professors. The findings revealed a highly contradictory dynamics of the motivational sphere across different years of study. While the majority of students maintain a responsible attitude toward their education, the direct cognitive interest, internal learning drive, and emotional satisfaction from the process significantly decrease from junior to senior courses. This drop in intrinsic motivation is gradually replaced by purely pragmatic and formal factors, such as the necessity of passing exams, external attendance control, and future career competitiveness. Based on the results, the key conditions for fostering sustainable intrinsic motivation were highlighted: ensuring intellectual independence, creating problem-based situations, offering a differentiated task system, encouraging freedom of choice, and implementing innovative teaching approaches. The practical value of the work lies in proposing over twenty specific interactive methods to enhance students’ motivational sphere through optimized teacher-student partnership.

items.title: Trust, relationships and impact: Evidencing the human work of learning designers
items.abstract: Learning designers (LDs) play a critical role in supporting higher education teaching and learning, especially through periods of significant digital change, from the rapid transition to online learning during COVID-19 to the redesign of learning and assessment in response to generative AI. In this increasingly digital and AI-enabled higher education sector, learning design is inherently relational, requiring practitioners to meet academics where they are and support educational change through trust, collaboration and compassion. Yet much of this work remains hidden, and difficult to articulate and demonstrate using traditional institutional measures. While output metrics such as consultations, workshops and resources developed provide evidence of activity, they often fail to capture the relational, collaborative and transformative nature of LD practice. Drawing on King and Patterson’s (2026) conception of course design as an act of care, we argue that many of the most significant contributions of LDs are relational rather than transactional. To address this challenge Boreland et al. (2025) developed the Learning Design Evidence Framework (LDEF) which provides a structured approach to evidencing the relational work underpinning educational innovation. The framework makes visible how LDs build trust, foster collaboration, influence practice, and create the conditions for meaningful educational change using seven segments; Student-Centered Design, Curriculum Design and Innovation, Professional Development, Promotion and Sharing of Quality Design, Scholarship of Teaching and Learning, Leadership and Influence, and Recognition and Reward. Across each segment, meaningful impact is demonstrated through collaboration, partnership and sustained engagement with academics, students and institutional stakeholders. Together, the segments provide a structured approach to evidencing the breadth, depth and relational impact of LD practice. This interactive poster invites the ASCILITE community to inform what constitutes meaningful evidence of LD impact, drawing on diverse institutional contexts and practices across the sector. The poster itself is designed to be conversational, inviting delegates to contribute their perspectives by responding to three reflective prompts: What evidence do you think demonstrates the value of relationships and human connection in LD? What contributions of LDs have you noticed are often overlooked or invisible? What evidence do you see as most important in the future? Using pens and markers, or sticky notes, delegates will collectively build a visual representation of the evidence they value, the invisible work they recognise and the future directions they envision for the profession. This participatory approach reflects the framework’s emphasis on co-creation, reflective practice and shared understanding while creating opportunities for meaningful discussion among delegates from diverse institutional contexts. By the conclusion of the conference, the poster will have evolved into a collective representation of how the LD community values evidence, relationships, and impact. In doing so, it will demonstrate that the future of LD is not defined solely by digital technologies, but by the human connections that enable educational transformation.

items.title: Uncertainty and proportionality when artificial intelligence forecasts trigger environmental restrictions
items.abstract: Some environmental regulators now trigger restrictions on forecasts before exceedances occur, while machine-learning methods are proposed for the forecasting pipelines behind them. Delhi-NCR’s Graded Response Action Plan (GRAP) directs advance invocation on numerical air-quality forecasts, yet reported practice often followed observed readings. Judicial and regulatory directions demand anticipatory action, yet none reviewed here specifies the confidence a forecast must carry before it justifies coercion. This article asks what validation, reproducibility and uncertainty-quantification thresholds an AI-enabled forecast must meet before triggering binding restrictions. Using a functional comparative method, it separates physics-based forecasts and digital dissemination from the machine-learning layer that makes a pipeline AI-enabled. GRAP, with the Supreme Court’s timing orders, is the single test case. Instruments from India, China, France and California’s air districts are coded for observed, forecast-based and discretionary triggers and read alongside forecast-verification studies. This article argues that proportionality and reasoned decision-making require restrictions to reflect forecast confidence as well as predicted severity, and that precaution licenses early action only if uncertainty is disclosed. One implication is that legal reliance on an AI-enabled forecast should depend on a disclosed validation dossier, because machine-learning layers add opacity and drift. Disclosure supports human oversight and lets affected people contest restrictions built on overconfident models. The contribution is a test mapping calibrated confidence onto the intensity of proportionality review. The assessment is prospective and doctrinal, evaluating design adequacy rather than operational performance; conclusions remain contingent.

items.title: Understanding Posttraumatic Growth Following Lifetime Trauma: Longitudinal Latent Class Analysis Including Cognitive Processes
items.abstract: The nature of posttraumatic growth (PTG), defined as positive changes that can occur after a traumatic event (TE), is debated due to its complex and dynamic relationship with psychological adjustment. Although heterogeneous PTG trajectories have been identified, the processes underlying their development over time remain insufficiently understood. This study, adopting a person-centred approach, seeks to identify latent classes with distinct multivariate trajectories (PTG, PTSD, positive thinking, deliberate rumination) over 1 year and their sociodemographic, event-related, and psychosocial determinants. A sample of 244 adults exposed to a TE completed, at three points spaced 6 months apart, online questionnaires assessing PTG and psychosocial variables. Sociodemographic and event-related characteristics were collected at baseline. Latent classes with distinct multivariate trajectories were identified. Analyses of variance, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression tested differences between classes and their predictors. Three classes emerged: Constructive PTG (25%), Struggling PTG (45.5%), and No PTG (29.5%). Differences between classes were observed in age, coping, challenge to core beliefs, positive illusions, depression, and social support. Lower baseline adaptive coping predicted membership in the Struggling and No PTG groups, whereas lower challenge to core beliefs predicted the No PTG class. These findings highlight the heterogeneity of trajectories following lifetime trauma and the role of coping and cognitive engagement processes in the evolution of PTG over time. By integrating multiple processes within a longitudinal, person-centred framework, this study contributes to a more nuanced understanding of the perceived PTG.

items.title: Understanding students’ GenAI usage, attitudes, and training needs for equitable and sustainable AI adoption in higher education
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is expected to revolutionise Australian’s economy with the potential to generate up to $600 billion per annum to GDP by 2030 (Australian Government, Department of Industry, Science and Resources, 2024). To keep up with the accelerating growth of AI, the higher education sector needs to transition from traditional teaching models to an AI-integrated pedagogy. One of the key concerns in this transition is to ensure equitable and sustainable adoption of AI in higher education. This concern is in line with the UNESCO’s recommendation on the ethics of AI (UNESCO,2021). AI adoption in higher education is both complex and consequential, as it may affect educational ethics through economic disparities among students and heterogenous student attitudes towards task fulfillment (Oxfam, 2022; Vacarelu, 2023). Moreover, it is reframing teaching, learning and assessment design, making it increasing difficult to distinguish between authentic effort, mastery, and output (Mills et al., 2025). Undertaken at an Australian university, this research project aims to addresses two pressing questions in contemporary higher education: how students are currently using generative AI (GenAI) for everyday learning tasks, their attitudes towards it and their AI readiness to support transition towards equitable and sustainable engagement with these tools. By revealing these issues, this project ensures student voices are central to ongoing debates about AI in higher education. Hence, this study is both equity-focused and evidenced-based as it responds to a critical gap for evidence-based insights to inform institutional policy development for a more equitable and sustainable digital ecosystem. Best practice suggests that when policies affecting students are designed with their involvement as co-designers, outcomes significantly improve. Therefore, framed as Scholarship of Teaching and Learning (SoTL) research, the project places reflective practice and systematic inquiry at the heart of continuous improvement in teaching and learning outcomes. This study uses a quantitative survey method, whereby a structured questionnaire was administered during semester one, 2026. The questionnaire design is based on the Digital Divide and Self-regulated Learning framework. Data were collected from Humanities students across Law, Accounting, Business, and Education disciplines. Results reveal widespread adoption (98%), with some of it uncritical and potentially over-reliant (similar to Palmer, 2023). Notably, outliers exist where students refuse to use the tools entirely. Overall, findings indicate variation in GenAI usage, attitudes, access, and competence, suggesting the need for targeted interventions to advance equitable and sustainable AI integration. The findings are useful as they inform student-centred teaching practices, curriculum design, and policy frameworks aligned with the university’s commitment to innovative, ethical, and inclusive education.

items.title: Unfolding autonomy: the action area of experienced autonomy of individuals in agile project teams
items.abstract: Agile project teams promote autonomy, yet little is known about how individuals actually experience autonomy in their day-to-day work. Building on a multiple-case study of five organisations in a manufacturing context with 61 semi-structured interviews, this study analyzes how individuals experience autonomy in agile project work. Drawing on the critical incident technique, complemented by an associative imagery technique, the paper presents a conceptual model of the action area of experienced autonomy, which unfolds through seven interrelated themes: decision-making, owning, realising, information sharing, learning, supporting, and team organising. The analysis of five cases shows how individuals make sense of this action area, revealing autonomy as a relational, contextual, and situational phenomenon. This study contributes to research on autonomy in management research by advancing the understanding of relational autonomy in agile project teams. It highlights autonomy as an experienced action area rather than a static job design feature or motivational characteristic. For managers structuring agile work in production and engineering environments, the findings offer a diagnostic lens to reflect on and support autonomy, fostering a motivating work context. Methodological contribution is achieved by demonstrating the value of associative imagery in capturing abstract and partly tacit aspects of work experience in agile production and engineering contexts.

items.title: Value-Recontextualizing Decision Support (VRDS) Experiment 2: Cognitive Value Recontextualization and Adaptive Preference Alignment in Human-AI Moral Decision-Making
items.abstract: This preregistration describes Experiment 2 of the Value-Recontextualizing Decision Support (VRDS) project, a PhD study at Florida Institute of Technology. Decision-support systems are usually judged by the quality of the outcome they recommend, rarely by whether a decision fits the decision-maker's own values. VRDS treats a choice that goes against a person's earlier values as a signal worth examining. It uses two mechanisms. Cognitive Value Recontextualization (CVR) shows such a choice from another point of view: a different framing of the situation, and a person affected by the choice. Adaptive Preference Alignment (APA) asks the person to clarify their priorities before the system updates its picture of their values. In the project's first experiment (N = 52), the full CVR+APA condition gave the highest value consistency without a measurable loss in performance. This experiment tests whether that holds in a larger sample and across several moral domains. Design. An online, between-subjects experiment with four conditions in a 2 × 2 design (CVR present or absent × APA present or absent): CVR+APA, CVR only, APA only, and Baseline (neither mechanism). The server assigns each participant to the condition with the fewest participants so far, so the four conditions stay balanced. All participants first answer four short blocks that measure their values. They then make choices in six moral scenarios: a chemical-leak evacuation, a wildfire evacuation, a limited cancer-treatment allocation, cuts to home-care visits inside an employer's rules, the same cuts decided by someone else, and a city repair rule chosen behind a veil of ignorance. Finally they see a summary of their own choices and answer feedback questions. The study takes at least 35 minutes. Participants. 104 adults recruited and paid through Prolific (26 per condition), plus students of one artificial intelligence course at Florida Tech who may take part for course credit (about 50). Hypotheses and expected outcomes. 23 hypotheses in four families, each with one primary hypothesis. (A) Conditions: participants in CVR+APA will make choices more consistent with their own values (Value Consistency Index, VCI) than participants in Baseline. (B) Position: how far a choice departs from a person's values will differ between deciding the care-visit cuts inside an employer's rules and receiving the same cuts decided by someone else. (C) Prediction: the system's Moral Prediction Function will predict the rule each participant chooses behind the veil of ignorance, before seeing the prediction, more often than chance (25%). (D) Performance: when a first pick goes against the participant's values and a reflection, clarification or confirmation step follows, the final choice will perform equivalently to the first choice (within ±5 points on a 0-100 scale). The four primary hypotheses are Holm-corrected together.

items.title: Verifying Agents in Rubric-Graded Environments
items.abstract: As AI agents take on increasingly open-ended and complex tasks, verifying their outputs has proven to be difficult. Rubric-graded agent environments, where a verifier judges multiple natural-language criteria against the deliverables and environment state changes produced by the agent, have emerged as a popular paradigm. We conduct the first systematic study of verifiers for rubric-graded agent environments. First, we create BankerVerifierBench (BVB), a meta-evaluation dataset of 2,464 human-judged rubric criteria across 24 investment-banking tasks. Next, we develop a methodology that derives from any rubric corpus the capabilities a verifier should possess, yielding a nine-capability taxonomy that we distill into three general design principles---reactive verification, environment alignment, and domain guidance---which we implement in Gandalf, an open-source verifier. Finally, we evaluate Gandalf against three existing verifiers on BVB. Gandalf matches or exceeds every baseline's F1 at lower cost: with Gemini 3 Flash it matches the strongest baseline's F1 (0.864 vs. 0.852) at one-fifth of its cost, and with GPT-5.4 models it improves F1 by over 0.12 at lower cost. Gandalf also generalizes to OpenClaw, a structurally different personal-productivity environment, where it again achieves the highest F1 (0.955 vs. 0.934 for the best baseline). We release BVB, Gandalf, and the code and data to reproduce our experiments.

items.title: VeriMath: Human-in-the-Loop Generation and Verification of Curriculum-Aligned Mathematics Assessment Items
items.abstract: Automatic generation of mathematics assessment items is a growing area in educational artificial intelligence, yet classroom deployment remains challenging. Generated questions must satisfy multiple constraints: mathematical correctness, curriculum alignment, appropriate cognitive difficulty, and educator reviewability. While prior work has advanced text generation, reliable assessment authoring requires granular control over localized examination formats and expert educational judgment. To address this challenge, we present VeriMath, a generalized, human-in-the-loop framework for generating rigorous, curriculum-constrained mathematics assessment drafts. Using annotated reference items, the framework anchors generation to the requested examination section and cognitive reasoning level, then applies sequential automated verification and guided repair before submitting drafts for expert review. We evaluate VeriMath through a national curriculum case study using 4,555 mathematics items from the Vietnamese Grade 12 curriculum and 50 distinct generation requirements covering multiple-choice, true/false, and short-answer formats. Across two model backbones, the framework produces verifier-accepted drafts for 94% (47/50) of requirements per run. Blind expert evaluations confirm high mathematical accuracy and curriculum alignment, with strict teacher-readiness assessments accepting up to 56.8% of generated items. Analysis of rejected drafts reveals persistent domain-agnostic challenges involving formatting, statement validity, and solution-step completeness. These findings demonstrate that VeriMath can bridge generative AI and dependable educational applications by producing highly reviewable assessment drafts within tightly constrained national curriculum frameworks.

items.title: Visual foundation models with adapter learning for Parkinson’s disease recognition based on OCT images
items.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) images have emerged as a promising means for PD recognition. However, constructing a precise DNN-based PD recognition model requires a large number of OCT images and expensive computational resources. This paper aims to transfer pre-trained visual foundation models (VFMs) with the aid of the adapter learning paradigm to recognize PD from OCT images, by adding only a few trainable parameters. We propose a novel VFM-Adapter framework for automatic OCT-based PD recognition based on the adapter learning paradigm. To be specific, we introduce three lightweight adapters: global adapter, local adapter, and token-wise adapter, to effectively leverage the transferability of feature representations from VFMs to OCT images, for equipping VFMs with strong PD recognition capability. Our VFM-Adapter achieves an accuracy of 77.66%, sensitivity of 78.01%, specificity of 77.31%, F1-score of 77.93%, and precision of 79.58%. It outperforms state-of-the-art deep neural networks, such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), attention-based CNNs, and vision transformers by updating only a small number of parameters. Extensive ablation studies further demonstrated the effectiveness of each adapter. The proposed VFM-Adapter provides an effective yet parameter-efficient transfer learning framework for OCT-based PD recognition. By substantially finetuning the small number of trainable parameters while maintaining competitive PD performance, the proposed framework offers a promising altetnative for automated PD screening in real-world diagnosis scenarios. items.title: VITAL: A Framework for Validating Agentic AI in Pharmaceutical Drug Development and Clinical Trial Operations
items.abstract: Current assurance approaches do not establish whether evidence is sufficient to validate, monitor and govern agentic artificial intelligence (AI) within a pharmaceutical context of use. Plausible outputs may conceal failures in retrieval, reasoning, orchestration or human-control points, where reference standards are unavailable. We developed and operationalised VITAL (Validation by Intended use, Traceability, Autonomy and Lifecycle evidence), a validation framework for agents in clinical development, through landscape analysis, regulatory and standards mapping, expert interviews and multi-stakeholder refinement. VITAL integrates context of use, controls, behavioural validation and lifecycle evidence within a risk-adjusted framework. We applied VITAL across epidemiology and treatment-landscape analysis, site selection, enrolment rescue and trial-design trade-off support to translate autonomy, reversibility, transparency and patient impact into proportionate validation activities, evidence requirements and auditable reconstruction of system behaviour. VITAL may inform evidence requirements and lifecycle accountability for higher-risk pharmaceutical uses; evaluation should assess reproducibility across assessors, organisations and system configurations.

items.title: VIVID: Beyond Static Multi-Image Reasoning with Localized Visual Differences and Textual Entity Dynamics in Video MLLMs
items.abstract: Video question answering under tight frame budgets requires preserving localized motion and event order, yet current video multimodal large language models (MLLMs) reduce comprehension to static multi-image reasoning by discarding unselected frames and encoding keyframes independently: (1) Spatially, whole-frame pooling dilutes small moving targets into static backgrounds; (2) Temporally, dropping intermediate frames or averaging tokens erases inter-frame motion, confusing direction, speed, and order. We propose VIVID (Visual Inter-frame Variations and Individual Dynamics), which moves beyond static snapshots like human vision: keyframes capture core states while inter-frame Patch Diffs preserve neighboring changes within $K_f$ keyframes. Autonomous Delta-Driven Keyframe Planning (ADKP) selects anchors from a $3\text{ fps}$ pool and feeds surrounding patch differences into Dual-Road Change Memory (DRCM), forming Dynamic Tokens at zero extra anchor tokens alongside a camera-stabilized Active Motion Region of Interest (ROI) and chronological Entity State Chains. Adding $0.22\%$ trainable parameters to a frozen $27\text{B}$ backbone, VIVID-Small ($50$ examples, $\sim 1.5$ GPU hours) beats all eleven baselines in overall accuracy across $8,083$ questions and trails only VIVID-Large ($3,600$ examples), which leads on MotionBench, Video-MME, and TempCompass.
topics: Generative Adversarial Networks and Image Synthesis

items.title: VRLLM: Turning LLMs into Powerful Tabular Classifiers
items.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on text, but whether pretrained LLMs are effective for large-scale tabular classification remains unclear, as many previous works demonstrate that LLMs' tabular data classification performance falls behind tree-based models or neural architectures designed for tabular data. At Visa Research, we managed to fine-tune a pretrained Llama 3.2 1B LLM on billions of rows of labeled tabular data and make it outperform a wide array of tabular classifiers and even our competitive production deep learning model. For ease of reference, we refer to the model as the Visa Research LLM (VRLLM). In this paper, we share how we achieved this exciting result, covering data preparation, training recipe, ablation studies of design choices and deployment validation. We also benchmark frontier LLMs on the same task and analyze their prediction behavior across model families and generations. Our interpretability experiments suggest that VRLLM learns feature-specific predictive associations, while component ablations indicate that the earliest two FFN layers contribute to the emergence of linearly decodable task information. Our paper provides an engineering recipe and a focused empirical case study on adapting compact LLMs to industrial tabular prediction tasks.

items.title: WATERFALL: Workflow for Adaptive Training with Evolutionary Reward Formulation and Automated Learning Loops
items.abstract: Reward design remains a central bottleneck in reinforcement learning (RL), particularly in sparse-reward, long-horizon and partially observable settings requiring dependency chaining, memory, and deceptive affordance disambiguation. While recent foundation-model approaches reduce manual reward engineering, most assume goal-conditioning, task descriptions, expert demonstrations, or ground-truth metrics. These assumptions are problematic in partially observable environments, where task-relevant objectives, affordances, and dynamics must be discovered through interaction rather than disclosed a priori. We formalise this problem setting by introducing WATERFALL, an iterative population-based workflow for automated reward discovery under the strict observability constraints inherent in POMDP environments. WATERFALL achieves this by (i) synthesising diverse programmatic reward candidates via persona-conditioned generation, (ii) evaluating candidate behaviour from raw visual rollouts utilising a Swiss-system evolutionary tournament judged by vision-language models to identify elites, and (iii) leveraging longitudinal assessment histories to iteratively mutate, escalate, or prune candidates. We evaluate WATERFALL across fully observable and reveal-gated partially observable environments ranging from discrete to continuous, comparing against sparse-reward RL, intrinsic-motivation and foundation-model reward-synthesis baselines. Our results indicate that WATERFALL discovers and refines reward programs without access to privileged information, outperforming baselines that retain their native information advantages, most clearly in the POMDP regime. Extensive ablations substantiate that visual evidence, tournament-based selection, and iterative refinement are jointly important. Enforcing this contract is what separates autonomous reward discovery from benchmark-privileged reward shaping.

items.title: Website-Facing Disclosure Obligations and Compliance Signals for Crypto-Asset Service Providers: A Cross-Jurisdictional Legal Mapping
items.abstract: Crypto-asset service providers increasingly meet users through websites, wallet-connect flows, and other public interfaces, but the legal duties attached to that visible layer remain fragmented across licensing, AML/CFT, marketing, consumer-protection, privacy, tax, and stablecoin regimes. Existing comparative accounts usually map regulatory perimeter and licensing architecture rather than the user-visible disclosure layer. This article maps de jure obligations and legally relevant compliance signals at the public interfaces of crypto-asset service providers across twenty-two jurisdictional units, using FATF standards and selected international policy materials as reference points. It develops a 15-category matrix that separates binding duties, conditional legal duties, inferred supervisory signals, prudential signals, and areas where no website-facing requirement was identified. The article treats the website as a regulatory disclosure interface and offers a structured starting point for jurisdiction-specific legal analysis, regulator-facing guidance, and future empirical audits of actual website compliance. A separately stated normative proposal connects consumer choice and entrepreneurial freedom to a country-of-origin regime for functionally integrated online services, with responsibility allocated across human–machine systems and agent-mediated interactions. This proposal is distinguished from the legal mapping and is not presented as an existing international exemption.

items.title: What AI can and cannot do: A cognitive-depth framework for differentiated AI integration in higher education
items.abstract: Higher education has responded to generative AI largely by regulating it by task, specifying where the technology may or may not be used in each assessment. This paper argues that task-based regulation uses the wrong unit of analysis. A single task typically spans several types of cognitive work, and a tool that can be welcomed for one type may quietly displace another. This conceptual paper proposes a four-level framework of cognitive engagement, adapted from classical Chinese expressions about knowing and articulated in contemporary cognitive terms: broad knowledge acquisition, analogical transfer, contextual inference, and original creation. The levels are ordered along a single axis, from cognitive work that is codifiable and reducible to rules and patterns, to work that is situated and dependent on human judgement. This axis maps closely onto the boundary of what generative AI can and cannot do: capability is near-complete at the codifiable end and degrades sharply as work becomes situated. The framework thus functions as a diagnostic lens for design, allowing educators to assign AI a role matched to the cognitive work a task is meant to develop. Two illustrative cases show the framework guiding differentiated, defensible decisions about AI integration within a single assessment.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

items.title: What Does an Agent Need? Bundle-Aware Agent Resource Composition
items.abstract: An agent resource's value depends on its backbone and companion resources and is known only after execution. Token-based generators remain tied to their training catalog, while independent resource scoring misses complementarities and reused bundles target other tasks. We formulate Task-Conditioned Agent Resource Composition (AgentComposition): jointly selecting a backbone model and a tool-skill bundle to maximize end-to-end execution utility. Our Retrieval-Grounded Bundle-Aware Agent Generation retrieves candidate resources and past configurations of similar tasks. A fine-tuned generator reads resource descriptions and recombines candidates through constrained beam search, allowing new resources without retraining. A bundle-aware critic ranks complete configurations using a large language model (LLM) teacher and historically successful configurations as execution proxies, and adapts to execution feedback when available. We evaluate reference recovery, offline execution with judged and native rewards, and online recommendation with real execution, building AgentSelect-Exec with 5,060 executed configurations. Our method recovers the complete reference configuration within ten candidates for 67.73% of AgentSelect queries, nearly twice the strongest baseline, and leads all baselines on SkillsBench. The proxy-trained critic raises the top-ranked agent's execution score from 7.58 to 8.37 out of 10; execution feedback increases it to 8.78, above the strongest baselines. Four target-domain queries suffice to adapt the generator to SkillsBench. Agents recommended online outperform the strongest baselines under both an LLM judge and native verifiers. These results support learning and transferring joint resource composition from task experience.

items.title: What holds and what breaks: Boundary objects in AI-enabled curriculum governance
items.abstract: Universities govern AI adoption through artefacts. Policies, rubrics, assessment briefs, vendor evaluation frameworks, and design templates cross organisational boundaries and carry meaning differently in each context. This paper applies the concept of boundary objects within a cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework to analyse which artefacts effectively mediate AI governance across academic, institutional, and commercial activity systems, and which fail. Drawing on the author’s framework for negotiated legitimacy in interacting activity systems and reflexive practitioner experience as an education design leader, the paper develops a typology of AI governance boundary objects classified by origin, interpretive flexibility, and failure mode. The analysis identifies three structural conditions that determine whether a boundary object supports or undermines the legitimacy of learning designers who broker AI adoption across systems. These are co-design across activity systems, support for transformation rather than coordination alone, and resistance to capture by a single system’s logic. It also identifies a failure dynamic specific to generative AI, in which an unstable referent causes artefacts to decay. The paper offers practical design principles for governance artefacts and connects them to a wider question, namely how institutions keep human and pedagogical judgement central as they adopt digital technologies.

items.title: What makes AI educational? A sociocultural framework for transforming AI from artefact to mediating tool
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet much of its use positions AI as a private productivity tool for generating answers, feedback or text. This paper argues that AI is not educational simply because it produces outputs. From a sociocultural perspective, its educational significance emerges when pedagogical design transforms it from an artefact into a mediating tool for participation in disciplinary learning. The paper introduces the AI Mediated Participation Framework, grounded in mediated learning, appropriation and participation. It proposes three design principles: preserving learner ownership, scaffolding thinking through dialogue, and developing AI literacy through disciplinary practice. These principles operate through questioning, dialogue, reflection, critical evaluation and decision making to support learner agency, evaluative judgement, responsible AI use, critical thinking and knowledge construction. The framework is illustrated through AI learning activities in undergraduate and postgraduate educational research courses, where educator modelling, peer discussion and disciplinary expectations repositioned AI from a private feedback service to a mediating tool for methodological reasoning and researcher judgement. The framework shifts attention from what AI can do to how pedagogical design determines what AI becomes educationally.

items.title: When AI Becomes a “Colleague”: How Anthropomorphism and Cognitive Support Shape the Demand-Cyberloafing Link in Human–AI Collaboration
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in the workplace, limited research has examined how job demands shape employees’ behavioral and motivational responses in human–AI collaboration and how resources influence these relationships. Drawing on Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) theory, this study adopts a mixed-methods approach, combining semi-structured interviews with 15 participants (10 employees and 5 graduate students) to explore relevant job demands and resources, followed by a cross-sectional survey yielding 282 valid responses to test the research model. The findings show that job demand is positively associated with cyberloafing and negatively associated with job engagement. Anthropomorphism strengthens the positive association between job demand and cyberloafing while weakening its negative association with job engagement. Cognitive support also strengthens the former relationship but does not significantly moderate the latter. These findings extend JD-R theory to human–AI collaboration by highlighting the differentiated roles of resources across behavioral and motivational outcomes. They also suggest that anthropomorphic AI may help sustain job engagement under demanding conditions, while its association with cyberloafing warrants careful consideration.

items.title: When AI Performs, What Remains? An Integrative Review of Generative AI and Cognitive Capital in Individuals and Organizations
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly entering knowledge work, and its short-term productivity benefits are increasingly documented. Less is known about what happens, over time, to the knowledge, skills, and judgment that remain in people and organizations. This integrative narrative review addresses that question through the construct of cognitive capital: the accumulated, renewable, and depletable stock of knowledge, cognitive, and metacognitive capabilities, and practices that enable an individual or an organization to learn, interpret information, exercise judgment, solve problems, and adapt. We distinguish individual and organizational cognitive capital from the capability of the human-AI system, so that gains in joint performance and losses in human capability can be observed at the same time. Drawing on experimental, field, and conceptual work, we propose four mechanisms through which interaction with AI affects cognitive capital: substitution of practice, scaffolding and feedback, metacognitive calibration, and organizational aggregation. Seven principles summarize the current evidence, including that assisted performance differs from retained competence, that the same technology can support or displace learning depending on design and use, and that individual gains can coexist with reduced collective diversity. For each mechanism, we derive testable propositions, and we discuss five design levers for organizations as proposals to be validated rather than established practice. We conclude that cognitive capital offers a multilevel frame for governing AI adoption and outline a research agenda centered on longitudinal, multilevel measurement.

items.title: When AI talks back: A cross-disciplinary study of educator design judgment in AI-assisted case development
items.abstract: Educators are increasingly turning to generative AI when developing teaching materials, yet most research to date has centred on student-facing applications. This paper presents a work-in-progress study that asks a different question: what happens to an educator’s design judgment when AI enters the case-writing process? Two business educators – one in accounting, one in management – will each develop a teaching case study using AI-assisted workflows, documenting their prompts, editorial decisions, and reasoning through structured process logs. Drawing on Schön’s (1983) reflective practitioner framework and Abell’s (1997) 10 criteria for effective teaching cases, the study examines where human expertise proves essential and where AI contributes meaningfully. The pairing of two sub-disciplines, management accounting and management, allows us to examine whether disciplinary knowledge shapes these design decisions in distinct ways, although the study’s central concern remain the design judgement itself. Early observations from the instrument development phase point to a useful distinction: AI appears better suited to qualities that require evaluative judgment (structure, data accuracy, length) than those demanding generative judgment (ambiguity, controversy, authentic voice). We expect further patterns to emerge once data collection begins. This paper outlines the research design and its anticipated contributions.

items.title: When connection requires refusal: AI backlash and accountable technology design in higher education
items.abstract: This non-empirical conceptual analysis examines how artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming woven into curriculum production, assessment, feedback, student support, academic integrity, accessibility and institutional decision-making. These systems are often justified through connection: faster feedback, personalised support, scalable services and more efficient learning design. Yet technical connection is not the same as educational connection. AI may leave the visible forms of university learning intact while weakening academic authorship, assessment validity, student trust, staff agency, care, equity and institutional legitimacy. The paper develops refusal-capable design: the distributed institutional capacity to decide when AI should be adopted, constrained, redesigned or refused. It integrates connected learning, responsible innovation, sociotechnical studies of educational technology, care ethics, justice-oriented educational judgment and technology non-use scholarship, using selected public examples illustratively rather than as an empirical sample. Six heuristic refusal zones organise recurring legitimacy tensions, and the Distributed Refusal-Capable University Design Cycle translates those tensions into accountable redesign. The contribution is a practical and theoretical account of refusal as a legitimate design outcome rather than simple opposition to AI.

items.title: When Do Typed Decision Models Work in Transportation? Evidence from Travel Choice and Traffic Signal Control
items.abstract: Typed decision models combine natural-language understanding with a structured interface that returns a selected action and an option-level probability distribution without generating lengthy textual responses. Their low inference cost and response latency make them attractive for transportation problems with predefined alternatives. This paper investigates their effectiveness, robustness, and efficiency in two representative transportation tasks: individual travel-mode choice prediction and sequential traffic signal control. We systematically evaluate TypeSafe Jev and GPT-6 Luna Decisions against conventional transportation methods, reinforcement learning algorithms, and four chat-based large language models. Experiments on the Swissmetro dataset show that typed decision models achieve lower prediction accuracy than traditional discrete choice models and the strongest chat-based baseline, while their performance varies substantially with input representation and question framing. In closed-loop traffic signal control experiments, typed decision models demonstrate competitive performance against established controllers in several scenarios, but exhibit performance degradation under more challenging network conditions. Furthermore, the typed models achieve lower inference latency and computational cost than the evaluated chat-based large language models, highlighting their potential for efficient, zero-shot transportation decision-making. Overall, these findings demonstrate both the potential and limitations of typed decision models, emphasizing the importance of input design, task characteristics, and robustness evaluation for their effective application in transportation systems.

items.title: When GenAI enters the assessment relationship: Public expectations of transparency, judgement and responsibility
items.abstract: Human-centred learning design requires more than using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) to make assessment feedback faster, more accessible or scalable. It requires attention to whether human judgement, relationships and responsibility remain visible when feedback is produced. The public is a key stakeholder in these decisions because university qualifications operate as public credentials whose legitimacy depends on confidence in how achievement is judged and certified. Yet debate has largely focused on students’ use of GenAI, with less attention given to public expectations of academic practice when GenAI contributes to feedback. This exploratory study surveyed 299 participants, most of whom had current or previous experience of higher education, to examine the implied obligations underpinning university assessment and feedback. Participants strongly endorsed feedback as an expected component of university teaching and generally supported disclosure of GenAI use, meaningful academic involvement and visible instructor responsibility. Exploratory factor analysis identified two provisional dimensions: AI feedback transparency and legitimacy, and assessment expectations and feedback value, although the second demonstrated only modest internal consistency. Interpreted through psychological contract theory, the findings suggest that human-centred GenAI implementation depends not only on feedback quality or efficiency but also on preserving visible academic judgement, accountability and educational purpose. The central design distinction is therefore between GenAI that supports academic practice and GenAI that substitutes for meaningful academic engagement.
