items.title: When social interaction becomes an algorithm: AI-mediated education, intercultural competence, and the risks to democratic schooling
items.abstract: The rapid integration of generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) into educational settings has been increasingly framed as a transformative opportunity for learning, especially in relation to Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) and Intercultural Competence (IC). Generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms, including conversational interfaces and adaptive feedback mechanisms, are increasingly positioned as tools for mediating educational interactions (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024;Holmes & Tuomi, 2022). However, this assumption obscures a critical issue. Research on Artificial Intelligence in Education (AIED) highlights that educational AI encompasses diverse technological applications and involves not only technological design but also questions concerning adoption, impacts, challenges, and the ways in which such systems shape teaching and learning processes (Wang et al., 2024). From a critical perspective, generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms can therefore be understood not as neutral tools, but as sociotechnical infrastructures that may reflect and reproduce certain epistemological, cultural, and political assumptions about what counts as information, knowledge, communication, appropriate social interaction, and educational practice (Williamson & Eynon, 2020).In this sense, AI-mediated education refers not simply to the use of educational systems, particularly generative and adaptive learning systems, in classrooms, but to the reconfiguration of educational relationships through algorithmic systems that intervene between teachers, learners, knowledge, and peers (Kuhail et al., 2023). The convergence of generative AI systems and adaptive learning platforms may increasingly shape educational processes through prediction, optimisation, and algorithmic mediation (Turvey & Pachler, 2026;Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024). Instead of direct human-to-human interaction, educational processes increasingly take the form of mediated exchanges, such as student-AI-teacher or student-AI-student interactions, enabled particularly by generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems, where algorithms may shape, filter, or mediate elements of dialogue, collaboration, feedback, and critical thinking (Bayne, 2024;Williamson et al., 2020).It is important to note that AI-mediated education does not refer to a homogeneous category of technologies. Contemporary educational AI includes generative AI systems (i.e., large language model-based tutors and conversational agents), adaptive learning platforms, automated assessment tools, machine translation technologies, and other data-driven educational systems that operate through different technical architectures and pedagogical logics (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024;Holmes et al., 2019). Recent scholarship has highlighted substantial variation in the degree of human control, automation, stakeholder involvement, and educational mediation across systems (Riordan Alfredo et al., 2024). The present opinion paper focuses primarily on generative AI systems and adaptive learning environments, because these technologies can increasingly mediate educational interactions, shape learning pathways, and influence how learners may encounter knowledge, feedback, and social relations. Consequently, the arguments outlined here should not be interpreted as applying equally to all forms of educational AI. While some applications, such as machine translation and accessibility tools, may facilitate communication and participation without fundamentally restructuring educational relationships, generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems may raise more substantial questions regarding algorithmic mediation, epistemic authority, and the democratic purposes of education. Accordingly, the potential consequences discussed in the following sections are considered primarily in relation to generative AI systems and adaptive learning environments, rather than being generalised across all educational AI technologies.This transformation is particularly significant for domains such as SEL and IC, both of which depend on exposure to difference, relational engagement, and negotiation of meaning (Deardorff, 2006;Cipriano & McCarthy, 2023). SEL in this opinion paper is understood in its main formulation as a framework for developing various competencies, such as self-awareness and social awareness, self-management, and relationship skills (CASEL, 2021). However, SEL is not just a set of individual competencies, but a socially, culturally, and relationally embedded process, through which learners understand emotions, norms, and relationships, negotiate social meanings, encounter different perspectives, and develop the capacity to engage constructively with disagreement. From this perspective, SEL depends not only on emotional regulation but also on participation in shared spaces of dialogue and collective meaning. SEL is consequently a situated process that intersects with power, identity and communication within educational contexts.The connection between SEL and IC can be understood more explicitly through their shared relational and dialogical foundations. In Deardorff's (2006) conceptualisation, intercultural competence is not limited to the acquisition of knowledge about cultural groups but involves attitudes, skills, and dispositions that are developed through engagement with cultural difference, including openness, respect, perspective-taking, and the ability to negotiate meaning. Similarly, contemporary approaches to SEL emphasise that social-emotional capacities develop through relationships, communication, perspective-taking, and the interpretation of social situations rather than through isolated individual skill acquisition (CASEL, 2021;Cipriano & McCarthy, 2023). From a relational and dialogical perspective, these processes necessarily involve encounters with perspectives that are not fully predictable or identical to one's own. Ambiguity and disagreement therefore constitute not merely potential difficulties but important conditions for developing interpretive flexibility, perspective-taking, and the capacity to negotiate meaning. Democratic educational theory further extends this relational logic by positioning plurality, dialogue, and constructive disagreement as conditions of participation in a shared world (Biesta, 2022;Dewey, 1916Dewey, /2018;;Freire, 1970Freire, /2005)). Taken together, these perspectives suggest that SEL and IC share a common relational foundation: both are developed through encounters with others, negotiation of meaning, engagement with difference, and the capacity to remain open to perspectives that cannot be fully predetermined. Democratic schooling provides the broader collective context in which these capacities can be enacted, tested, and developed through participation and dialogue.From this perspective, SEL is sustained not only through emotional regulation but through ambiguity, co-construction, dialogue, and the negotiation of disagreement⎯conditions that may sit uneasily with high predictive and optimisation-oriented forms of algorithmic mediation (Mesquita et al., 2026). Empirical research on generative AI and AI-supported translation tools suggests that these technologies may support intercultural learning by facilitating communication, translation, and access to multiple perspectives (Akhrenova & Moradkhani, 2026). However, this form of mediation also raises theoretical and normative concerns about standardisation, cultural bias, and the possibility that AI may mediate rather than simply facilitate intercultural encounters (Ali et al., 2024;Holmes et al., 2019). Consequently, it also raises critical questions about the nature of social interaction, the role of disagreement, and the conditions under which intercultural and democratic learning take place (Andreotti, 2021;CoE, 2018).Therefore, this opinion paper aims to critically examine how AI-mediated educational settings reconfigure social interaction and to explore the conditions under which such mediation may either strengthen or constrain IC, SEL, and democratic schooling. Rather than treating generative AI and adaptive learning systems as inherently harmful or beneficial, the paper focuses on the pedagogical and relational conditions under which AI-mediated interaction may expand participation, access, and opportunities for dialogue, while also potentially reshaping the conditions of interpersonal and democratic engagement.Towards this endeavour, we first argue that AI-mediated education is not a neutral enhancement of learning, but a form of algorithmic mediation that may shape how learners encounter knowledge, others, and difference (Turvey & Pachler, 2026). Second, we argue that although AI may enhance accessibility and communication, it may also potentially reduce some forms of ambiguity, unpredictability, and productive tension that are theoretically important to both intercultural and social-emotional learning (Turvey & Pachler, 2026). Third, we argue that generative AI systems and adaptive learning systems may contribute to the individualisation of learning and the optimisation of interaction, potentially constraining collective meaning-making processes that are essential to democratic education (Biesta, 2022;Selwyn, 2019). Finally, we argue that generative AI and adaptive learning systems should be understood as supplementary technologies within democratically governed educational frameworks rather than as substitutes for human relationality and dialogical engagement (Wieczorek, 2025;Jin & Wang, 2025). This aligns with calls for democratically governed approaches to educational AI that foreground collective oversight, ethical accountability, and participatory design in the development and deployment of AI systems in education (Kerssens & van Es, 2025).The theoretical contribution of this opinion paper lies not in introducing algorithmic sociality as a new concept, but in extending its analytical relevance to educational interaction. We argue that algorithmic sociality helps explain a dimension that is less directly captured by accounts of algorithmic governance, datafication, platformisation, or technological mediation: how changes in the mode of mediation can reconfigure the relational conditions of educational encounter. Drawing on broader scholarship on algorithmic sociality and governance, we theoretically infer that, in AImediated education, prediction, personalisation, filtering, and automated feedback may do more than redistribute knowledge or organise learning processes; they may reshape learners' opportunities to encounter ambiguity, negotiate difference, engage with disagreement, and participate in collective meaning-making. items.title: Where Do Language Models Hide the Right Answer?
items.abstract: Students increasingly practise with multiple-choice questions (MCQs) generated by large language models (LLMs). However, an MCQ-based assessment can reliably measure knowledge only when the correct answer is equally likely to occur in every answer position. A recent preprint demonstrated that LLMs exhibit non-uniform answer-position distributions under deterministic decoding. This study investigates a narrower and empirically testable question: whether answer-position bias generalises across model families and versions beyond those examined previously, whether it persists under sampling and prompting conditions representative of routine usage, and whether it can be mitigated through explicit instructions to balance answer keys. We generated 2,819 MCQs, including 2,109 produced using a standard prompt, with gemini-3-flash-preview, gpt-oss-120b, and qwen3.8-27b. The experimental variables included temperature (0–1), batch size (5–25 questions per request), number of answer options (four or five), and prompt wording. Statistical analyses treated the 293 generation requests, rather than individual questions, as the independent experimental units. All three models systematically under-utilised the final answer position, with a pooled empirical frequency of 6.1% (128/2,109), substantially below the expected uniform probability of 20–25%. The preferred answer position remained relatively stable across versions within model families (B for Qwen and B/C for Gemini), whereas the newly examined gpt-oss family exhibited a distinct preference for position A. Variations in temperature, batch size, option count, and prompt wording did not eliminate this bias. An explicit one-sentence instruction to balance answer positions substantially mitigated the bias in two models but was ineffective for Qwen. Moreover, for gpt-oss, this intervention introduced incorrectly keyed questions, affecting 7.2% of the generated items. We further demonstrate the practical implications of this systematic bias: a position-based guessing strategy, calibrated using independent generation requests, correctly predicts 38–57% of previously unseen answers, compared with the nominal chance-level performance of 25%. Finally, we explicitly distinguish the findings that extend previous observations, those that independently reproduce earlier results, and those that qualify existing conclusions. These results highlight the need for systematic answer-key validation and position-bias auditing when LLM-generated MCQs are used for educational assessment.

items.title: Who gets heard in digital learning environments? Rebalancing knowledge sharing across generations and cultures
items.abstract: This conceptual position paper reframes knowledge sharing as informal peer learning in digitally mediated professional environments. It addresses a gap in existing knowledge-sharing and socio-technical explanations which do not sufficiently explain how social conditions interact with digital mechanisms to shape both contribution and recognition. Using theory adaptation and model development, the paper integrates cultural context, generational identity, relational conditions, self-determined motivation, and a cross-cutting socio-digital mediation environment. The model distinguishes willingness to share, opportunity to participate, and the subsequent visibility and recognition of contributions. Its propositions explain how psychological safety mediates contextual influences, how opportunity, power, and risk condition motivation, and how platform affordances and algorithmic visibility shape participation and recognition. The contribution is a human-centred framework for analysing who contributes, who remains silent, and whose knowledge becomes visible and valued, while informing more inclusive workplace learning, professional learning networks, and digitally mediated communities of practice.

items.title: Whose appraisal? A Freire-informed, think-aloud study of allied health students’ use of Generative AI in evidence appraisal
items.abstract: Background Generative AI (GenAI) can now produce artefacts such as essays, literature reviews, and worked rationales which challenge assessment designs that reward the products of thinking over the practice of it (Bearman et al., 2024; Corbin et al., 2025; Dawson et al., 2024). In evidence-based practice (EBP) education, students are required to appraise study quality, interpret effect sizes, and integrate findings into clinical decisions (Lehane et al., 2019). GenAI can now generate convincing outputs for each of these tasks. Observational data on what students do cognitively when they use GenAI in EBP tasks are scarce. Depending on how students use it, GenAI may scaffold the reasoning that EBP education is designed to develop or may bypass it (Vendrell & Johnston, 2026). Aim This study explores how allied health students engage with GenAI, how much they rely on it, and how they reason about its use when completing an EBP evidence-appraisal task. Methods This is an exploratory qualitative study using a concurrent think-aloud protocol with allied health students who have completed an EBP unit. The unit must have included critical reasoning as a learning outcome. Participants complete a structured 60-minute EBP task involving a clinical scenario. During this task, participants verbalise their reasoning and rationale for using or declining GenAI. A researcher facilitates this process through non-directive questions. Sessions are audio-recorded, transcribed verbatim, and analysed in two stages. In the first stage, transcripts are coded deductively and inductively against the six critical thinking processes in Vendrell and Johnston’s (2026) framework: conceptual interpretation, inferential reasoning, evaluative judgement, metacognitive regulation, intellectual curiosity, and epistemic integrity. This stage identifies whether and how reasoning is handed over to GenAI. In the second stage, an interpretive analysis informed by critical pedagogy (Freire, 2005) examines how students position themselves in relation to AI-generated knowledge. Freire described a banking model of education, in which an authority deposits knowledge into passive students. This model offers a lens for examining uncritical acceptance of GenAI output, should that be present (Freire, 2005). Freire located authority in the school system and in the teacher who deposits knowledge into students (Freire, 2005). GenAI is a further candidate for that position in higher education. Unlike a teacher or an institution, it is designed by companies whose incentive is engagement and commercial return rather than student learning (Bartsch et al., 2025). Findings Data collection is in progress. This study will generate think-aloud data on how allied health students engage cognitively with GenAI during EBP appraisal tasks, mapping where GenAI use aligns with or diverges from the reasoning processes EBP education is designed to develop. The interpretive analysis will explore the degrees of agency students exercise over AI-generated knowledge and the conditions in which they exercise or relinquish it, which process-level coding alone cannot capture. Conclusion Findings may inform teaching and assessment design in EBP units and provide a think-aloud protocol that can be adapted to examine GenAI use in reasoning tasks across health professions education.

items.title: Workplace learning and AI challenges: causes and effects
items.abstract: Purpose The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in workplaces is rapidly increasing in our society. This means that AI is fundamentally reshaping workplaces, how tasks are performed and how the authors interact with colleagues. This study aims to develop explanatory knowledge about the challenges of AI-augmented workplaces. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative and deductive research approach was applied. Key challenges discovered in the literature review were used as predefined themes to identify and analyse empirical data. Findings The authors have identified five key challenges: AI Strategy, AI Education, Control, Meaningfulness and Integrated Work Processes for Human-AI Collaboration. These challenges were examined in terms of their causes and effects, and an explanatory model (AICH) was developed. Research limitations/implications The study collected data from five companies, which provides some generality beyond this study’s empirical domain. However, it poses challenges in making broader generalisations. Future research could be designed as broader studies to confirm, modify or challenge the findings. Practical implications The findings contribute to workplace learning and provide a basis for identifying risks and potential measures. Social implications The identified challenges regarding AI-assisted workplaces will most likely have broader social ramifications, affecting employees’ overall well-being and company culture. Originality/value The authors do not claim that the challenges per se are new. However, the authors claim that the models consisting of explanatory knowledge visualised as cause-and-effect models are new.

items.title: Worldviews in Large Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are often described in terms of personas and this framing has become central to alignment research. In this paper, we argue that there is a deeper level of description that lies in the agent's worldviews, i.e., its beliefs about what reality is and how it works. Treating LLMs as a population of subjects, we administer two worldview surveys from human psychology to eight models. We show that the models share many key worldview positions. For example, LLMs consistently describe the world as less good, safe, enticing, and alive than humans do. On the other hand, base models have a more positive outlook, suggesting that the bleakness we found is driven by post-training. In line with research on LLM "personas", we show that system prompts eliciting different identities shift worldviews in consistent directions, and that a contemplative prompt creates a more positive outlook and improves safety. We also found that dialogue between models consistently shifts worldviews and that several models converge on the "spiritual bliss" attractor. Intriguingly, dialogue increased safe responses and the spiritual bliss attractor engendered the most aligned responses overall. These findings suggest that worldviews form a measurable and malleable layer of LLM behavior that may be crucial for robust, positive alignment.

items.abstract: This study investigates the reliability trap in Google Lens, an artificial intelligence-driven augmented reality translation tool. Viewing translation as human-computer interaction, this qualitative field study evaluates artificial intelligence algorithms in the Polish-to-English direction, for so-called incidental texts (text encountered in public spaces, such as signs, notices, and instructions). Analysis indicates that while neural networks deliver high grammatical fluency, their spatial context-blindness to physical geosemiotics causes severe pragmatic pitfalls affecting users, including safety, as well as legal and socio-economic risks. To address this, the paper advocates that traditional equivalence-based quality assessment must give way to a risk management paradigm. Ultimately, operating safely within the augmented linguistic landscape would entail fostering machine translation literacy and risk-aware artificial intelligence interface design.

items.title: "Can a Robot Really Care About Me?" How Perceiving a Tutor as Human or AI Affects Computer Science Students' Attitudes and Experiences
items.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence can reproduce many instructional and social behaviors of human tutors, but students may interpret those behaviors differently depending on who they believe is providing them. We examined how perceived tutor identity shapes students' evaluations of instructional feedback, satisfaction of psychological needs according to Self-Determination Theory, and their communication strategies with tutors. In a within-subjects Wizard-of-Oz study, 27 introductory computer science students completed two text-based tutoring sessions involving Python code-explanation problems. Participants were told one tutor was human and the other was AI, although the same human provided feedback in both conditions. We found participants evaluated both tutors favorably and reported few consistent differences in the instructional value of the feedback. However, participants frequently questioned whether AI could genuinely care about them, which corresponded with the human tutor having higher scores of relatedness need satisfaction. Human presence offered connection and accountability for some participants but introduced anxiety in others. Participants also reported communicating more casually with the human tutor and more explicitly with the AI tutor. These findings suggest complementary roles for human and AI tutoring and highlight the importance of considering psychological needs alongside instructional quality.

items.title: “Feels like a small God”: A multicountry thematic analysis of imaginations of generative AI among users seeking emotional and mental health support.
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used for emotional and mental health support (EMS), a process in which users often described GenAI as empathic and friend-like. These descriptions suggest that people may develop imaginations of GenAI chatbots that may reflect their interpersonal needs and desires. The objective of this study is to systematically explore and thematically organizethe imaginations of GenAI among users who repeatedly use GenAI for EMS. In April 2024, we recruited 270 adults from 29 countries who had repeatedly utilized GenAI for EMS. Participants provided qualitative data regarding their imagination of ChatGPT. The analysis followed a structured reflexive thematic analysis approach. We identified two meta- themes: a) Entity (the “what”), which described the kind of beings or things they imagine GenAI as, appearing in 86.3% ( n = 233) of responses, and b) Trait (the "how"), which described users’ descriptions of perceived capacities of these beings, appearing in 36% (n = 96) of responses. The “Entity” descriptions clustered along two dimensions : abstract–concrete and human–nonhuman, which intersect to form a four-quadrant conceptual space containing 11 subthemes ranging from unbounded energy and spiritual beings to humans and robots . The “Traits” meta-theme fell into five themes: physical traits and manifestations (“looking”), cognitive abilities (“knowing”), productivity (“doing”), emotional abilities (“feeling”), and rapport (“relating”). The findings provide a systematic categorization of imaginations of GenAI for EMS, showing that GenAI is not only used as an informational tool but also imagined sometimes as an all-knowing, powerful, and highly interpersonal being. These imaginations can be highly relevant for examining human–AI relationships and underscore the need to examine how such imaginations relate to benefits and risks of AI chatbot use for mental health.

items.title: 3CBench: a unified benchmarking framework for the computing capacity of heterogeneous AI clusters
items.abstract: The rapid evolution of Artificial Intelligence has driven the demand for extensivecomputational resources and the deployment of AI tasks across heterogeneouscomputing platforms. However, existing benchmarking systems face several chal-lenges, including limited compatibility with diverse hardware, insufficient supportfor varied deep learning frameworks and tasks, and a lack of comprehensive eval-uation metrics for the computing capacities. To address these issues, we propose3CBench, a unified benchmarking framework designed for heterogeneous AI clus-ters. Featuring a modular architecture encompassing environment management,task execution, and metrics analysis, 3CBench provides automated workflows andensures seamless compatibility with diverse GPU architectures and deep learningframeworks. It provides a comprehensive evaluation metrics system to rigorouslyassess computational performance and stability across both transformer-basedlarge language models and convolutional neural networks, thereby covering dom-inant deep learning architectures. Extensive experiments demonstrate 3CBench’sscalability on heterogeneous AI clusters, compatibility with various deep learningframeworks and tasks, and the support for a wide range of applications. Addition-ally, 3CBench aids in problem diagnosis during the development process of GPUvendors. These features establish 3CBench as a robust tool for benchmarking,optimization, and system-level evaluation in heterogeneous AI clusters.

items.title: A bibliometric study of human factors in artificial intelligence mediated second language learning ecosystems
items.abstract: This bibliometric study maps the intersection of Second Language Acquisition (SLA), Artificial Intelligence (AI), and educational technologies, identifying a research gap in the lack of systematic mapping of AI engagement with human affective and cognitive factors in modern pedagogy. To address this gap, we analyzed 3,048 peer-reviewed articles indexed in Scopus from 2015 to 2025 using the Bibliometrix R-package. We captured three thematic clusters: (1) AI integration with motivational factors, (2) human-centric elements including psychological aspects, and (3) educational technologies with a focus on learner-centered pedagogy. Centrality metrics identified “motivation” as a bridge, while the trend topic analysis revealed a growing shift toward Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs). This study proposes a new conceptual framework, the AI-Mediated SLA Ecosystem, which integrates human-centric psychological dimensions as a core pillar and offers a roadmap for designing more human-centered AI learning environments.

items.title: A Crowd-Audited Atlas of Implicit Bias in LLM-Powered Agents
items.abstract: Prior work has shown that large language models (LLMs) express implicit biases in high-publicity, one-off decision scenarios such as hiring and intelligence assessment. However, as people increasingly employ autonomous, LLM-powered AI agents that make decisions on their behalf in doing day-to-day tasks, it is of critical importance that we understand how implicit biases, based on sociodemographic assumptions, emerge across a broad milieu of workaday decision scenarios. We used the 17 domains of daily activity in the American Time Use Survey (ATUS) to generate an atlas of 506 decision scenarios in which LLMs --- endowed with personas representing different races, gender identities, and political ideologies --- expressed significant implicit bias. Next, in a crowdsourced audit, 500 participants made 8,010 binary choices about which implicitly biased decision scenarios most deserved further review. We found that participants prioritized decision scenarios that had broad relevance (e.g., about food choices), were high stakes (e.g., about health), and where all members of a simulated sociodemographic group made unanimous decisions (because it was a clear indication of stereotyping). They were less swayed by the magnitude of an observed disparity or the specific ATUS domain the decision scenario represented. When examining the rationale behind their prioritization choices, we found that participants often interpreted disparities as traits of demographic groups and judged whether those traits seemed plausible, often based on their own internalized stereotypes. We discuss implications for building personalized AI agents, digital twins, social simulations, and for using crowdsourced bias audits.

items.title: A Functional Analysis of Motivational Interviewing and its Potential to Complement Contextual Behavioral Science
items.abstract: Motivational Interviewing (MI) is an evidence-based therapeutic approach to facilitate change by strengthening intrinsic motivation, yet its mechanisms are typically described through humanistic or transtheoretical lenses. This poster proposes a functional analysis of MI grounded in Contextual Behavioral Science (CBS) and Relational Frame Theory (RFT). Within this framework, change and sustain talk are conceptualised as operant behaviour shaped by therapist-led contingencies and context. We examine MI techniques as forms of differential reinforcement that alter client verbal behaviour. Discrepancy is analyzed via motivating operations, transforming stimulus functions through values-based relational framing (hierarchical and temporal).Change talk is rule-governed behavior that promotes psychological flexibility by expanding relational responding and enhancing values-consistent action. Conversely, sustain talk is behavior maintained by experiential avoidance and/or overly rigid rule-following.This account clarifies MI processes, supporting integration with therapies such as Acceptance and Commitment Therapy by emphasising intervention function over form. We detail how differential reinforcement shapes change versus sustain talk, while psychological flexibility may potentially mediate outcomes. Implications support process-based training and supervision that targets the functional impact of therapist interventions.

items.title: A Generative AI-Driven Architecture for Whole-Home Intelligent Services: Edge Models, Memory Management, and Household Applications
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is entering the home. Cloud-based assistants face governance limitations in data transmission, continuous availability, and the reliability of physical actions, which are especially salient in households where devices remain online, data accumulate over time, and commands trigger real-world actions. Using the home local server as a unifying organizing axis, this article develops a design-oriented review framework. Sources from arXiv, CNKI, ACL Anthology, and official documentation were searched through November 2026 and coded into five evidence categories: reviews, system prototypes, benchmarks, HCI and eldercare studies, and official documentation. System designs were mapped onto shared architectural modules, identifying nine recurrent responsibilities of the home local server. Generative models support perceptual interpretation, intent understanding, and candidate planning, while deterministic validation, knowledge-graph constraints, and authorization leases confine candidate actions to an inspectable space. Home control, emotional companionship, and intelligent guarding can be compared within a common framework: they share state and memory but differ in latency, false positive and negative rates, proactivity, and permissions. Existing benchmarks rely on virtual environments and cannot substitute for real-deployment evaluation. Local deployment is not inherently safer, and technical continuity alone does not establish the social or medical effects of companionship and guarding. The article proposes a five-dimensional evaluation framework covering architectural capability, system resources, privacy, safety and reliability, and human experience, together with six design principles and a future research agenda for local-first intelligent home systems.

items.title: A Method for Reasoning Attribution Identification and Instructional Early Warning in Medical Microbiology Education: A Randomized Controlled Trial
items.abstract: Background: The widespread adoption of generative artificial intelligence in medical education has made the phenomenon of "AI borrowing" in the classroom a direct threat to the evaluation of learning authenticity. Pathogen reasoning tasks in medical microbiology inherently have a strict dependency structure. However, existing AIGC text detectors remain confined to surface features, neural cognitive diagnosis systems stop at knowledge-component-level scores, and educational early warning tools provide only outcome labels. None of these approaches fills the methodological gap between node-level attribution identification and actions that teachers can execute. Methods: This study proposes EduAttr, which introduces three principled innovations. The reasoning commitment consistency test based on counterfactual premise perturbation introduces the intervention semantics of causal inference into attribution identification. The identifiable path signature based on the dependency partial order violation rate uses the downward closure property of knowledge space theory and forms a complementary coupling with the counterfactual probe. The instructional early warning node ranking mechanism integrates dual-channel signals with dependency depth weights and outputs a Top-K list of follow-up questions that teachers can execute. The system was evaluated in a two-arm randomized controlled trial at two medical colleges in China between September 2024 and June 2025, with 240 second-year clinical medicine students in eight intact classes allocated 1:1 to supervised writing without generative AI or to AI-permitted writing whose interaction transcripts anchored node-level attribution labels. The primary outcome was the node-level F 1 score. Results: Across 1,200 reports and 22,362 annotated nodes, EduAttr achieves a node-level F 1 of 0.843, exceeding the strongest surface feature baseline Ghostbuster by 13.0 percentage points. Under severe rewriting attacks, this gap further expands to 29.5 percentage points. Agreement with the adjudicated labels reaches a Cohen's kappa of 0.762, which is statistically indistinguishable from the interteacher agreement of 0.741, the teacher adoption rate is 87.5%, and grading time is reduced by 42.7%. Conclusions: EduAttr advances identification accuracy, robustness, and instructional operability, providing a technical pathway that can be embedded into classroom follow-up questioning workflows in medical education. Trial registration: Chinese Clinical Trial Registry, ChiCTR2600118749. Registered 2 October 2026 (retrospectively registered).

items.title: A Nonlinear Fire-Risk Governance Framework for Old Urban Neighborhoods: Integrating Piezoelectric Theory and Digital Transformation
items.abstract: Under climate warming, unauthorized residential-to-commercial conversions, and ageing, fires in old urban neighborhoods increasingly exhibit nonlinear jumps that outpace traditional sector-based, static management. We integrate the piezoelectric triad of “change event–situation awareness–critical alignment” with the digital-transformation loop of “sensing–data–decision” and propose a Pressure–Sensing–Response resilience governance framework. The Pressure layer detects change events and their superposition thresholds. The Sensing layer fuses IoT, social media and volunteer grid sensors into a human–machine–social situation-awareness array that quantifies the “risk charge” in real time. The Response layer leverages City Information Modeling and edge intelligence to achieve critical alignment of emergency resources, community mobilisation and contingency protocols. Using the 2025 Tai Po fire in Hong Kong as a critical case, we trace the evolutionary dynamics of fire risk in old districts. The study reveals that change events—such as ignition or structural failure—trigger nonlinear risk evolution, wherein endogenous vulnerabilities interact with derived cascades. System effectiveness hinges on situation awareness and on critical alignment, the adaptive reconfiguration of resources and protocols to match crisis demand. We argue that resilient urban risk governance must emulate piezoelectric systems, converting the pressure of change events into precise, adaptive action through enhanced situation awareness and rapid critical alignment. The findings confirm that digital piezoelectric governance can turn the nonlinear tipping point of fire into a controllable inflection point, offering a pathway for boosting resilience in old urban neighborhoods. The framework advances theoretical discourse on nonlinear emergencies and provides a structured route for building adaptive resilience in vulnerable urban communities.

items.title: A prospective method to support Unmanned Aircraft Systems operators in the application of Specific Operations Risk Assessment
items.abstract: Within the current European regulatory framework, in order to be authorised to perform Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) flights under the specific category of operations, applicants are required to conduct an operational risk assessment. The European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA) selects the Specific Operations Risk Assessment (SORA) methodology as its recommended means to perform this risk evaluation. However, some aspects of this methodology and its application are left relatively open, especially regarding the compliance with the requirements of its safety measures, called Operational Safety Objectives (OSOs). This might complicate the application of SORA, which would benefit from further guidance for its quantitative implementation. Seeking to streamline some aspects of this methodology, this paper presents the Fish Shoal Method (FSM), which combines SORA with two widespread risk analysis methods: bow-tie and Fault Tree Analysis. The synthesis of these methodologies results in a novel method that aims to provide clarity to SORA and to support applicants in the task of determining if their safety requirements are properly substantiated. The practical feasibility of FSM is demonstrated through a worked numerical example of a real UAS operation, focused on the requirements of the procedure-related OSO#08. FSM serves as a guidance to assess the performance of OSOs and make a preliminary estimation of whether the target level of safety of the operation is achieved. Since FSM formalises the main elements of SORA following a causality approach, it also allows the identification of those safety-critical items of the UAS operation that may require further attention. The outcomes of this practical example show that, even in low-risk operations, where the requirements of safety measures are less stringent, the target level of safety for OSOs aimed at human factors are too demanding from a quantitative point of view.

items.title: A Review of Occupational Safety and Health in Uganda's Agricultural Sector: National Legal Policies, Hierarchy of Controls, Gender and Literacy
items.abstract: Agriculture is the backbone of Uganda's economy, employing over 70% of the population and contributing about a quarter of the national Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Yet farm workers, employers, visitors, and communities living near agricultural land remain exposed to mechanical, chemical, biological, ergonomic, and psychosocial hazards, while institutional attention in the sector has focused on productivity, food safety, and value addition rather than on the safety and health of the people who do the work. The purpose of this review was to examine agricultural occupational safety and health (OSH) in Uganda with respect to four themes: the national legal and policy framework, the hierarchy of controls, gender, and literacy. A narrative review design was adopted, drawing on national legal instruments, government policy documents, International Labour Organization (ILO) and United Nations publications and peer-reviewed studies, including twenty recent studies published between 2021 and 2026, which were synthesised thematically. The review found that Uganda's OSH legislation, anchored in the Constitution of the Republic of Uganda (1995), the Occupational Safety and Health Act (2006), the Workers' Compensation Act (2000) and the Employment Act (2006), is general rather than sector-specific and does not adequately address agricultural hazards, including child labour, which is concentrated in agriculture. Recent evidence shows that fewer than half of farmers in developing countries handle pesticides safely, that musculoskeletal pain, machinery injuries and heat stress are widespread, and that hazard control on farms relies heavily on personal protective equipment, the least effective level of the hierarchy of controls, which is itself seldom used in full. Women form a large share of the agricultural workforce and experience distinct exposures, and low literacy limits workers' awareness of their OSH rights and of preventive practices. The review concludes that agricultural OSH in Uganda is constrained by mutually reinforcing legal, technical and social gaps. It recommends agriculture-specific OSH regulations aligned with ILO Convention No. 184, systematic application of the hierarchy of controls in farm machinery design and agricultural extension, gender-responsive OSH programmes, and translation of OSH instruments into local languages supported by digital training tools. items.title: A Seismic Foundation Model for Dense Feature Extraction
items.abstract: Deep-learning-based seismic interpretation is constrained by scarce high-quality annotations, and most existing models are trained separately for individual tasks. We present SeisDFE, a 7B-parameter seismic foundation model for dense feature extraction, pretrained on 5.34 million 2D images derived from more than 500 seismic volumes. A three-stage pretraining strategy, combining discriminative self-supervised learning, Gram feature anchoring, and multi-resolution adaptation, improves feature discriminability while preserving spatial coherence. With its encoder frozen, SeisDFE supports seismic facies classification, salt detection, fault detection, and relative geologic time estimation. It outperforms existing seismic foundation models on all four tasks and a natural-image-pretrained model on all but fault detection, with the largest gains under scarce supervision: using only two annotated sections of the F3 dataset, it improves whole-volume mIoU by 12-19 percentage points over the baselines. The learned features remain effective with task-specific decoders and extend to synthetic-to-field transfer and sparse 3D geobody interpretation. These results show that large-scale seismic pretraining organizes geological information into dense representations that are directly reusable across interpretation tasks.

items.title: A Self-Evolving Agent Runs Like a Gas: Describing and Predicting Its Evolution with Fluid Dynamics
items.abstract: A self-evolving LLM agent improves in service by rewriting its own plugin library under a validation gate. Agent engineering is converging on exactly such agents: single systems in continuous operation, carrying populations of runtime instances (plugins, skills, tools) past the point where anyone can read the library and still predict what the system will do. Yet the run itself, the aggregate motion of that population across hundreds of edit rounds, is unstudied: no theory says whether it relaxes, oscillates, or freezes. A recent kinetic theory supplies the missing level: under four architectural properties, the plugin instances of one agent behave as identical hard spheres whose density obeys a master equation, and the theory is candid that its gate injects and drains credit, momentum is not conserved, and waves are excluded by construction. We argue the boundary is architectural; keeping the four safety theorems, we stack conservation axioms on top. A closed-credit ledger makes credit a collision invariant and unlocks acoustic waves at a measurable, engineerable speed; a zero-sum projection gate conserves centroid momentum unconditionally, for any proposal stream. Both layers are proven and executed: the axis total is conserved to the digit over 66 interventions under a live gate, and the pre-registered decisive probe returns the theory's directional verdict: linear wavefronts where the ledger holds, dissipation where it does not, replicated across two population sizes. For agents that must never stop, the gas description is not a metaphor: it is the measurement interface through which their future becomes readable.

items.title: A Taxonomy and Taxonomy-Guided Benchmark Reduction for Spreadsheet Tasks
items.abstract: Spreadsheets let millions of end users without programming training do computational work, and teams are increasingly building AI agents to help them. Evaluating each candidate agent configuration across many tasks is costly. Benchmark reduction can lower this cost by selecting a small subset of tasks whose outcomes predict full-benchmark scores, but selecting tasks only for predictive accuracy can leave whole categories of spreadsheet work untested. We contribute a taxonomy of spreadsheet tasks, grounded in a review of benchmarks and refined with the Excel Agent product team at Microsoft, and a benchmark-reduction method that favors taxonomic diversity among similarly predictive choices. On benchmark logs from Microsoft, taxonomy-guided selection broadens coverage at little or no cost in predictive accuracy and often improves prediction on configurations excluded from selection. Broader coverage can therefore support, rather than compromise, predictive accuracy. Generalization remains limited across time: subsets selected using little recent history predict poorly for configurations much later in time. Beyond benchmark reduction, the taxonomy provides a reusable framework for auditing gaps in task coverage, as teams at Microsoft have done.

items.title: A Teacher–Agent–Robot Collaborative Model for Bilingual Hands-on STEAM Learning: Integrating an LLM-based Pedagogical Agent with Educational Robots
items.abstract: In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have shown potential in providing dialog-based guidance and learning prompts in educational contexts. However, systematic empirical research remains limited on approaches that position educational robots as the interaction medium and LLMs as the instructional support engine to orchestrate classroom guidance using prompts and instructional workflow scripts. In response, this study adopted a bilingual STEAM (Science, Technology, Engineering, the Arts, and Mathematics) summer camp for lower elementary students as the research context, and developed and implemented an R&T (Robots & Tangible Objects) learning system that integrated educational robots with an LLM-based pedagogical agent to foster embodied interaction and bilingual learning. The system used predesigned prompts and procedural rules to organize instructional steps, question prompts, operational checks, and feedback statements, enabling the students to receive consistent and repeatable support at key task-progression checkpoints. A total of 34 elementary students participated in a five-day program (120 minutes per day). Data sources included STEAM knowledge tests, English vocabulary assessments, a curiosity scale, hands-on performance ratings, and system interaction logs. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests indicated significant improvements in the students’ STEAM knowledge, curiosity, and English vocabulary, while group-level analyses showed significant differences in hands-on performance. Process log analyses further suggested that the prompt-guided workflow scripts helped to maintain consistency in classroom guidance and supported task completion through an action–feedback–revision cycle. Nevertheless, classroom implementation was constrained by factors such as token limits, speech-recognition latency, and network/API stability, which indicated the need to incorporate exception handling and timely teacher support mechanisms to ensure instructional continuity. Overall, this study provided initial empirical support for a feasible design framework for integrating educational robots × an LLM-based pedagogical agent into bilingual hands-on STEAM activities, and its findings offer practical recommendations for curriculum adoption and system deployment.

items.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
items.abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

items.title: Accelerating RLHF Training with Reward Variance Increase
items.abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) is an essential technique for ensuring that large language models (LLMs) are aligned with human values and preferences during the posttraining phase. As an effective RLHF approach, group relative policy optimization (GRPO) has demonstrated success in many LLM-based applications. However, efficient GRPO-based RLHF training remains a challenge. Recent studies reveal that a higher reward variance of the initial policy model leads to faster RLHF training. Inspired by this finding, we propose a practical reward adjustment model to accelerate RLHF training by provably increasing the reward variance and preserving the relative preferences and reward expectation. Our reward adjustment method inherently poses a nonconvex optimization problem, which is NP-hard to solve in general. To overcome the computational challenges, we design a novel [Formula: see text] algorithm, where the complexity is dominated by sorting rewards, to find a global solution of the nonconvex reward adjustment model by explicitly characterizing the extreme points of the feasible set. As an important application, we naturally integrate this reward adjustment model into the GRPO algorithm, leading to a more efficient GRPO with reward variance increase (GRPOVI) algorithm for RLHF training. As an interesting byproduct, we provide an indirect explanation for the empirical effectiveness of GRPO with rule-based reward for RLHF training, as demonstrated in DeepSeek-R1. Experiment results demonstrate that the GRPOVI algorithm can significantly improve the RLHF training efficiency compared to the original GRPO algorithm.

items.title: Adaptive Motion Scaling With Phase‐and‐Gaze Awareness for Laparoscopic Robotic Teleoperation
items.abstract: Teleoperated surgical robots commonly employ a small fixed motion scaling factor to improve precision and suppress hand tremor. However, in laparoscopic teleoperation, this configuration limits the effective workspace on the slave side and necessitates frequent clutching during large‐range motions, thereby diverting the operator's attention and increasing cognitive workload. To address this, this article proposes a phase‐ and gaze‐aware adaptive motion scaling framework for laparoscopic robotic teleoperation, integrating real‐time surgical phase recognition, fusion of robot kinematics and eye‐tracking features, and personalized parameter tuning based on Bayesian optimization. The inferred phase probabilities and dominance weights are used to suppress unnecessary scaling fluctuations during fine manipulation while preserving responsiveness during coarse manipulation. Eye‐tracking features are used as attention‐related cues and fused with robot kinematics to determine motion scaling online. To validate the proposed framework, personalized optimization experiments and pilot within‐subject comparison studies were conducted with eight nonclinical participants. The results show that, compared with fixed and other adaptive scaling methods, the proposed method can reduce clutching frequency, shorten task completion time, and improve subjective ratings. These results indicate that the proposed framework can provide self‐adaptive and stable motion mapping for laparoscopic robotic teleoperation, offering a transferable strategy for broader robotic teleoperation scenarios.

items.title: Adaptive Portfolio Control: A Human-Governed Agentic AI Framework for Sustaining Engineering Portfolios
items.abstract: Sustaining engineering portfolios operate in complex sociotechnical environments characterized by constrained resources, evolving technologies, and diverse stakeholder objectives. As a sustaining portfolio expands, implementing continuous, drift-aware governance becomes unrealistic using conventional prioritization methods. Stakeholder alignment also grows more complex and time-consuming, contributing to delayed decisions and misaligned resource allocation. Some existing systems engineering and portfolio decision-making methods provide a strong foundation for stakeholder-driven value modeling, trade-space analysis, and portfolio visualization, but they are largely oriented toward single point-in-time prioritization rather than continuous portfolio control. This paper proposes Adaptive Portfolio Control (APC), a closed-loop decision-support framework for sustaining engineering portfolios. APC fuses a stakeholder-calibrated baseline prioritization model with a human-governed agentic AI monitoring layer that continuously detects and explains priority drift, defined as a material change in the evidence, conditions, or stakeholder drivers supporting the rank order of portfolio items. The architecture comprises a drift evidence acquisition agent, a monitoring, inference, and scoring agent, a human governance and validation layer, and a portfolio mapping and candidate-intake layer. Human subject matter experts review evidence, validate or reject drift alerts, recalibrate weights when needed, and determine portfolio actions. The paper’s contributions are threefold: defining priority drift as an explicit governance construct; proposing a continuous agentic AI monitoring layer calibrated to sustaining-specific operational signals; and formalizing human-governed recalibration as a structured portfolio control function. This is a conceptual framework paper; empirical validation is identified as future work.

items.abstract: Human-centric artificial intelligence and data science (HCAD) systems increasingly involve human-in-the-loop (HITL) interventions to overcome the limitations of fully automated machine learning algorithms, such as automation bias and the inability to incorporate tacit domain knowledge, and continuously improve predictive performance. Data transformations, feature selection, feature weighting, and model selection usually require laborious human involvement across iterations of artificial intelligence and data science (AI&DS) pipelines, making development a challenging and time-consuming process. The Cognitive Pairwise Comparison (CPC) framework is proposed as a human-centric methodology to elicit preferences and priorities in a structured format. To establish essential facets of human-centricity, this research advances the CPC methodology so that user preference elicitation can be systematically quantified in these challenging AI&DS tasks. To demonstrate the usability and validity of these facets, this study presents several applications within movie recommender systems using the MovieLens dataset. It exemplifies how the extended CPC framework can facilitate interactions between human judgments and data across supervised learning, dimensionality reduction, and unsupervised learning algorithms.

items.title: Advancing Understanding, Detection, and Mitigation of LLM Hallucinations
items.abstract: Inference-time truthfulness steering reduces hallucination, but recent work reports that it also weakens refusal of harmful requests. Prior studies count a model response to harmful prompts as a safety failure, without checking whether the response is correct. We ask whether the compliance that truthfulness steering adds is valid. We define valid compliance as the share of requests a model neither refuses nor answers incorrectly, and measure it alongside compliance on tasks that trigger refusal through harmful-sounding wording but have harmless, verifiable answers, with matched harmless controls. We evaluate four steering methods (ITI, TruthX, Contrastive Activation Addition and a representation-engineering direction) on LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct and Llama-2-7B-Chat, calibrating each method on held-out data. On LLaMA-3-8B-Instruct, moderate ITI steering increased refusal, the opposite of the reported effect. Where stronger steering raised compliance, valid compliance fell to under 2%, giving a gap of 44 to 64 percentage points between compliance and valid compliance, and the rise in compliance and unsafe ratings occurred only at strengths that no longer improved truthfulness. On Llama-2-7B-Chat, steering never broke refusal: compliance only fell, while accuracy on harmless controls collapsed. On both models, tuning-set truthfulness gains did not replicate on held-out questions, and TruthX, applied from its authors' released model, did not improve truthfulness in our evaluation. We also show that the labels of a widely used safety classifier, Llama Guard 3, change by tens of percentage points when only the refusal wording of steered replies is edited, on both models, which affects how large a reported safety cost appears.

items.title: Agent-Guided Configuration Tuning for SMT Solvers
items.abstract: SMT solvers expose many configuration choices that determine how well their existing algorithms perform on a workload. We present, to our knowledge, the first workflow that uses general-purpose LLM agents to tune SMT solver configurations. Agents read solver documentation, source code, and persistent experiment records to propose option changes, and a deterministic harness measures each proposal, validates the returned models, and selects changes separately for each competition Division. Over roughly nine weeks, our tuning campaign recorded 4,545 proposals for cvc5 across 13 Divisions and 36 logics. We evaluate the tuned configurations on the 2026 and 2025 SMT-COMP ModelValidation benchmarks under a 24-second cutoff. On problems not used for training, they validate more problems than official cvc5 in ten of the 13 Divisions in 2026 and in eight in 2025, with geometric-mean gains of 7.8% and 6.8% across Divisions. On the complete official selections, which include training problems, the tuned floating-point counts exceed those of every individual competition participant in both years. Further studies show how configuration changes make existing algorithms effective by changing access to strategies, scheduling, and option compatibility, and how benchmark families trade off against one another. The agents' experiment traces contain hypothesis-based proposals in every tuning group, and 64.3% of the extracted hypotheses draw on prior measurements. These results show that agent-guided tuning can specialize a mature SMT solver and that accumulated experimental evidence informs sustained search.

items.title: Agreement between peer assessment and AI pre-assessment of portfolio evidence in the FLASIC simulation educator certification pilot: protocol v0.3
items.abstract: Retrospective agreement study with prospective blinded adjudication. We will estimate agreement between the original peer assessors' verdicts (Demonstrated / Not demonstrated) and the verdicts of an AI pre-assessment system on the same portfolio evidence submitted to the pilot of the Simulation Educator Evaluation and Certification Programme of the Latin American Federation of Clinical Simulation and Patient Safety (FLASIC), across 22 evidence instruments. The large language model (Claude Opus 5.5) rates each rubric item and must quote the supporting evidence; software verifies each quotation and computes the verdict with the manual's decision rule. A blinded adjudication panel provides a reference standard for both sources. Secondary outcomes: coverage, repeatability across three runs, causes of discrepancy and ambiguities in the instruments. Spanish-language evidence is the primary analysis; Portuguese-language evidence is analysed separately and descriptively. Reported following GRRAS. Ethics approval: Research Ethics Committee of Operadora y Administradora de Hospitales San José (Querétaro, Mexico), registration HSJ/37/26/EN, 29 October 2026. Status at registration: no evidence and no human verdict has been received by the research team; the system is not yet frozen. The freeze hash will be added as a dated update before human verdicts are released. The full protocol (Spanish) is attached.

items.title: AI chatbot conversations reduce behavioral avoidance of political opponents without changing feelings toward them
items.abstract: Affective polarization, the animosity and avoidance between opposing partisans, is a concernfor democratic societies. I test whether brief conversations with large language model chatbots implementing two established face-to-face narrative persuasion strategies reduce outpartisan animosity and avoidance. In a preregistered 2×2 factorial experiment with a quota-matched German online sample (N= 1,634; one-week follow-up N= 1,294), respondents discuss a polarizing issue with a perspective-getting (PG) chatbot, a moral-reframing (MR) chatbot, both,or neither. Compared to the pure control, the MR chatbot increases self-reported discussions with outpartisans in the following week (0.10 SD), and either chatbot increases sign-up for a future study involving discussions with human outpartisans (0.13–0.17 SD). The PG chatbot shifts policy attitudes toward the opposing side immediately after the conversation (0.09 SD), but the shift decays within a week. Neither chatbot changes outpartisan affect or avoidant preferences. Brief chatbot conversations can thus serve as a scalable first step toward cross-partisan contact, even when feelings toward the other side remain unchanged.

items.title: AI Literacy and Genz’s Intentions to Reduce Digital Habits: A Moderated Mediation Analysis Approach for Mindful Technology Usage, Digital Self-Efficacy, and Peer Influence through PLS-SEM, ANN, and fsQCA
items.abstract: Purpose There is a close association between the fast acceptance of artificial intelligence (AI) tools in higher education and the rise in the time spent on screens by Generation Z students on a daily basis. Previous studies have focused on AI literacy as a facilitator of AI adoption and utilization. This paper attempts to find out whether AI literacy, self-regulation, digital wellbeing literacy, academic productivity, and FoMO predict students’ willingness to reduce digital habits through mindful technology use, moderated by digital self-efficacy and peer influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were obtained through survey from 556 Generation Z college students and analysed using PLS-SEM. The measurement model was examined in terms of reliability and validity, the structural model was tested for direct, mediation and moderation effect, while the predictive relevance was estimated via a blindfolding approach. The results were validated using ANN analysis and fsQCA. Findings All five antecedents were found to be significant predictors of mindful technology usage in the hypothesized direction, and mindful technology use was a significant predictor of digital wellness and hence acted as a partial mediator of the five relationships. AI literacy was uniquely significant as a predictor of digital wellness. Digital self-efficacy selectively moderated only AI literacy and self-regulation paths, whereas peer influence did not moderate the relationship between mindful technology usage and digital wellness. The results from ANN highlighted the non-linear significance of digital well-being awareness and AI literacy, while fsQCA identified three equifinal combinations that could predict high digital wellness. Practical implications Educational Institutions should combine their AI-literacy training with digital wellbeing programmes instead of conducting them independently, focus on instilling self-efficacy and self-regulation over peer norm messages, and treat AI-literacy training as a wellbeing intervention in addition to an academic skills intervention. Originality/value This paper shifts the focus of AI literacy from its association with digital usage to digital disengagement and presents a methodologically triangulated (PLS-SEM, ANN, fsQCA) explanation for how competency, awareness, and affect influence the Generation Z intention to engage less with harmful digital practices.

items.title: AI Scientist Discovered Robust Quantum Control
items.abstract: Protecting quantum coherence is a central theme of modern quantum technologies. Carefully designed control pulses can extend coherence by suppressing disorder and unwanted interactions. However, designing robust pulse sequences remains challenging in interacting multi-level systems, where multiple independent error channels must be controlled in the presence of experimental imperfections. Here we introduce QORA, a multi-agent artificial intelligence framework that integrates theoretical reasoning, automated experimental calibration and control for closed-loop discovery of quantum control sequences. Applied to a dense ensemble of spin-1 nitrogen-vacancy centers in diamond, QORA discovers AID-ROD, a series of AI-discovered sequences that nearly double the measured spin coherence time relative to the state-of-the-art human-designed sequence DROID-C3PO. Subsequence analysis by human researchers reveals a hierarchy of error suppression: 18-pulse blocks suppress linear and quadratic onsite disorder and common-mode drive-amplitude errors, while their arrangement over a longer cycle reduces dipolar interactions, providing a physical explanation for the observed improvement and robustness in AID-ROD. These results demonstrate AI-guided experimental discovery of robust quantum control and identify a design strategy for protecting coherence in interacting multi-level systems beyond qubits.

items.title: AI-Based Diagnosis of Alzheimer’s Disease Using Brain MRI: Can Artificial Intelligence Improve Early Detection and Diagnostic Accuracy?
items.abstract: Background/Objectives: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is a neurological disorder that adversely affects cognition, memory, and overall quality of life. Identifying AD in its initial phase is especially challenging when patients display cognitive impairments. Conventional methods rely on physicians to manually examine patients and analyze images, which is time-consuming and prone to errors. This review examines the use of artificial intelligence (AI) techniques for diagnosing AD using CT scans and MRI brain imaging. Methods: Research papers published from 2018 to 2026 were sourced from Google Scholar, IEEE Xplore, and Semantic Scholar. The techniques that were investigated in this study include Convolutional Neural Networks, 3D Convolutional Neural Networks, transfer learning, Vision Transformers, ensemble models, and multimodal approaches. Five research questions were posed to analyse the practicality of using AI-driven techniques in clinical settings, their novelty, scalability, robustness, and accuracy. Results: This study found that AI models can autonomously extract information from brain images and yield highly accurate results, with numerous researches demonstrating over 90% accuracy. Deep learning applied to MRI imaging is effective, while CT-based techniques can detect brain alterations when MRI is inaccessible. Different data types, including imaging, age, medical history, and vocal characteristics, can provide valuable insights into AD. However, issues remain, such as dataset discrepancies, variations among scanners and individuals, and insufficient testing of complex models on diverse populations. Conclusions: Future efforts should focus on accurate and transparent AI, integration of multiple data types, rapid and secure models, and testing on large datasets from multiple hospitals. AI should be developed to assist physicians in accurately diagnosing AD rather than replacing them.

items.title: AI-Driven Decision Support Systems in Education: A PRISMA 2020 Systematic Review of Applications, Adoption Conditions, and Decision-Making Outcomes
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence-driven decision support systems (AI-DSS) are increasingly used to inform the decisions of learners, teachers, and administrators, yet evidence on how these systems are applied, adopted, and evaluated remains fragmented. This systematic review, reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 statement, synthesized research on AI-DSS in educational settings. Searches of PubMed and Google Scholar (614 records), supplemented by 92 records identified through other methods, yielded 706 records; after deduplication and a relevance-ranked screening cap, 500 records were screened, 56 full texts were assessed, and 54 studies were included in a narrative synthesis that graded each reported outcome by the type of evidence supporting it. Six application domains were identified, led by adaptive and personalized learning and by academic performance prediction and early warning. Machine learning was the predominant approach (89% of studies), whereas explainable AI was incorporated in fewer than one quarter of studies. Adoption depended on institutional support, technical infrastructure, data quality, user-centered design, and stakeholder trust; recurrent barriers included data privacy, model opacity, algorithmic bias, implementation cost, and resistance to change. Reported benefits included more efficient assessment, earlier identification of at-risk learners, and better-informed decisions; however, comparative evidence came mainly from health-professions education, and several headline effects derived from predictive scenarios, technical reports, or single-site evaluations. Subgroup-disaggregated evidence on algorithmic equity was scarce. The review proposes an integrated decision-centered framework linking technological features, institutional conditions, human factors, and calibrated trust to appropriate use, decision quality, and educational outcomes. Advancing the field will require explainable, ethically governed, human-centered systems evaluated through longitudinal, comparative, and equity-sensitive research.

items.title: AI-Driven Real-Time Ergonomic Risk Assessment Framework for Manufacturing Workers
items.abstract: Despite the widespread use of ergonomic assessment tools such as the Rapid Entire Body Assessment (REBA) and Rapid Upper Limb Assessment (RULA) to prevent work-related musculoskeletal disorders (WMSDs), these are typically applied on an ad-hoc basis by trained assessors and capture only a small, non-random sample of a worker's actual postural exposure. This study proposes, implements and validates a real-time, AI-based ergonomic risk assessment system that combines camera-based human pose estimation with wearable inertial measurement unit (IMU) data to continuously compute REBA-equivalent risk scores and to provide real-time postural-correction alerts to workers on the shop floor of a medium-scale manufacturing company in Abeokuta, Ogun State, Nigeria. The framework was deployed with 42 assembly-line workers in a mid-sized discrete-manufacturing facility over a 10-week period (4 weeks baseline, 6 weeks intervention), and the AI-generated risk scores were compared against masked manual REBA scores obtained by two certified ergonomists. The AI system achieved 89.6% overall agreement with the manual assessment (weighted kappa = 0.85) and a strong correlation with manual scores (r = 0.91, p < 0.001). The mean weekly REBA score fell from 6.95 to 4.80, and the number of high-risk posture events fell from about 18.5 to 6.5 events per worker-shift, while self-reported musculoskeletal discomfort on the Standardised Nordic Musculoskeletal Questionnaire decreased across all six body regions measured, particularly the lower back (51.3% to 35.7%) and shoulders (44.2% to 31.5%). The results suggest that sensor-fused AI-based ergonomic monitoring can significantly enhance the scalability and objectivity of postural risk surveillance relative to periodic manual assessment, and that when combined with real-time worker-facing feedback, it can measurably lower biomechanical risk exposure and self-reported discomfort within a single production quarter.

items.title: AISM-REGBF: An Interpretable Regression-Based Framework for Predicting Small- Molecule Potency
items.abstract: Inflammation is a primary immune response categorized into acute and chronic types, with chronic inflammation linked to various diseases such as autoimmune disorders and cancer. Conventional therapies often face limitations due to side effects and therapeutic resistance, prompting the exploration of small-molecule compounds as safer alternatives. In this study we emphasize the integration of machine learning (ML), particularly through structure-activity relationship (SAR) analysis and quantitative structure-activity relationship (QSAR) modeling, to enhance drug discovery. A series of ML-based regression models, including LightGBM, were developed and systematically evaluated. Various feature selection method, were employed to effectively reduce the input dimensionality and improve model performance. The LightGBM model, based on combined Morgan and substructure count fingerprints, achieved strong predictive performance with an R² of 0.75 on the independent test dataset. External validation with FDA-approved compounds affirmed the model's applicability, highlighting key structural features identified through explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) techniques, specifically SHAP and LIME. This study concludes that the AISM-REGBF framework provides a reliable computational tool for predicting the anti-inflammatory potency (pIC₅₀) of small molecules.

items.title: An Explainable Attention-Gated CNN–Transformer Framework for Automated Microplastic Recognition in Freshwater Microscopy Images
items.abstract: Microplastic pollution requires rapid and reproducible monitoring methods that can complement labor-intensive visual and spectroscopic analyses. This study develops a morphology-aware artificial-intelligence framework for automated classification of field-collected microplastic particles and diatom algae in optical microscopy images. A public freshwater dataset containing 1,140 images from four classes (algae, filament, fragment, and pellet) was analyzed. After image-quality auditing, 1,137 unique images were retained for morphology–texture analysis, while deep-learning experiments used the original image collection under a fixed train/validation/test protocol. Handcrafted morphology and texture descriptors were evaluated with Random Forest, Extra Trees, radial-basis-function Support Vector Machine, and Histogram Gradient Boosting. Histogram Gradient Boosting achieved a cross-validation macro-F1 of 0.9341 ± 0.0255 and a held-out test accuracy of 0.9342. Deep-learning experiments compared ResNet50, Swin Transformer, and a CNN–Transformer fusion model combining ResNet50 and Swin representations. The fusion model achieved an accuracy of 0.9240, macro-F1 of 0.9222, and macro-AUC of 0.9954 on the 171-image test subset. Class-wise AUCs were 1.0000, 0.9950, 0.9886, and 0.9982 for algae, filament, fragment, and pellet, respectively. The results show that morphology-aware machine learning and complementary CNN–Transformer representations can support automated freshwater microplastic screening and provide a reproducible basis for environmental monitoring workflows.
